arakhin.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · VALUATION, MEASURE, DEDICATION
arakhin.title: Read a vow whose legal shape comes from a fixed measure.
arakhin.intro: Arakhin follows vows that assign a valuation to a person. Track the Torah’s schedule, the categories that control it, and the conditions that modify payment without erasing the underlying measure.

sessions.title: A person named for valuation
sessions.translation: valuation of a person · vow · dedication
sessions.prompt: What pressure does the opening case create?
answers: It asks how a vow about a person becomes a defined Temple dedication.
It says a vow has no legal consequence unless an object is handed over immediately.
It treats the person named in the vow as ordinary market property.
sessions.feedback: Right. Arakhin makes the vow a legal case: a person is named, but the obligation is expressed through a valuation.

sessions.title: A fixed schedule, not a guess
sessions.translation: fixed valuation · according to the years
sessions.prompt: What should a reader identify before calculating the obligation?
answers: That the Torah supplies a fixed valuation schedule with defined categories.
That each person may choose any amount that feels appropriate.
That the valuation is determined only by local market price.
sessions.feedback: Good. The fixed schedule is the legal mechanism; it prevents the vow from becoming an open-ended estimate.

sessions.title: Age and category matter
sessions.hebrew: מבן חודש ועד בן חמש · ערכך
sessions.translation: from one month through five years · your valuation
sessions.prompt: Why does the source divide people into age categories?
answers: The category determines which fixed measure applies to the vow.
Age is mentioned only as narrative background and never changes the amount.
Every age category receives the same valuation by definition.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A careful reading tracks the factual trigger because the schedule changes with the category.

sessions.title: The named person is not the number
sessions.translation: the vow · the valuation · the dedication
sessions.prompt: What distinction should remain visible?
answers: The person named, the fixed valuation, and the dedication are related but distinct legal elements.
The valuation number replaces the person and makes the original vow irrelevant.
A dedication has no structure beyond the speaker’s private intention.
sessions.feedback: Right. The map preserves the legal sequence: vow, measure, then dedication.

sessions.title: From where does the schedule come?
sessions.translation: from where are these words? · your valuation
sessions.prompt: What does a Gemara source-question invite here?
answers: Ask which Torah wording authorizes the fixed valuation categories.
Replace the Mishnah with a modern pricing rule.
Ignore the repeated Torah phrase because it is only stylistic.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Gemara turns the schedule into a proof question, tracing legal categories back to the Torah’s wording.

sessions.title: A measure with limits
sessions.hebrew: ואם מך הוא מערכך · על פי אשר תשיג יד הנודר
sessions.translation: if he is too poor for your valuation · according to what the vower can afford
sessions.prompt: What should a reader test after finding the fixed measure?
answers: Which condition modifies the payment while leaving the valuation category intact.
Whether poverty erases the original category and the entire vow.
Whether a fixed schedule means no circumstance can ever matter.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Scope work asks how the source preserves the category while allowing a defined condition to affect what can be paid.

sessions.title: Historical dedication law
sessions.translation: to learn · to understand · to ask
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of these valuation sources?
answers: Study their categories and reasoning as historical textual literacy, not as a current fundraising tariff.
Treat the ancient schedule as a practical instruction for modern charitable pledges.
Avoid the legal reasoning because Temple dedications are historical.
sessions.feedback: Serious study can honor the source while clearly distinguishing its historical dedication system from contemporary practice.

sessions.title: Map a measured vow
sessions.translation: category · valuation · condition · result
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new valuation-vow case?
answers: Name the category, identify the fixed valuation, test any modifying condition, then state the resulting obligation.
Choose an amount first and use the source only to justify it afterward.
Treat the person, the valuation, and the dedication as one interchangeable fact.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Arakhin by tracking category, fixed measure, condition, and consequence in order.

avodah-zarah.pageTitle: Jewish Learning Academy · Avodah Zarah Arc
avodah-zarah.kicker: NEZIKIN SOURCE TRAIL · TIME, COMMERCE, CONTEXT
avodah-zarah.title: Read a boundary rule without erasing its history or its neighbors.
avodah-zarah.intro: Avodah Zarah asks how commercial and ritual boundaries are defined in a particular ancient setting. Learn to map the action, reason, exceptions, and historical context before making any modern comparison.

sessions.title: A restriction with a calendar boundary
sessions.hebrew: לִפְנֵי אֵידֵיהֶן שֶׁל עוֹבְדֵי כוֹכָבִים שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים
sessions.translation: Before their festivals, for three days.
sessions.prompt: What should a reader notice first?
answers: The rule names a time window and a defined commercial setting.
It announces a timeless verdict about every person in another community.
It gives a private spiritual instruction with no legal structure.
sessions.feedback: Right. Start by locating the rule in time, action, and institutional setting.

sessions.title: Buying and selling are specific interactions
sessions.translation: It is prohibited to engage in commerce with them.
sessions.prompt: Why name the action precisely?
answers: The source defines a category of commercial interaction rather than banning every form of human contact.
The wording means that conversation, hospitality, and friendship are all automatically forbidden.
The action is only symbolic and has no legal significance.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A careful reader keeps the named transaction distinct from broader social questions.

sessions.title: Benefit, exchange, and presence are not one category
sessions.translation: Commerce · benefit · presence.
sessions.prompt: What is the best reading move when related restrictions appear?
answers: Track each category separately before asking whether a later source connects them.
Treat every neighboring word as proof that all forms of contact have identical status.
Ignore distinctions because the topic is too historically distant.
sessions.feedback: Good. Legal reasoning depends on knowing which action a category actually names.

sessions.title: The Gemara tests the reason
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: What does a reason-question invite the learner to do?
answers: Identify the concern the rule is addressing before extending it to a new case.
Replace the Mishnah with a modern opinion immediately.
Assume that one explanation settles every historical context.
sessions.feedback: Right. First recover the source's own concern; only then can comparison be responsible.

sessions.title: The source links commerce to festival practice
sessions.translation: Festival day · benefit · support.
sessions.prompt: How should the stated concern be represented?
answers: As a claim about whether a transaction materially supports a prohibited public practice in that setting.
As a claim that every person in the surrounding society has the same intention.
As proof that historical circumstances never affect legal interpretation.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Keep the source's economic and ritual concern visible without making claims about every individual.

sessions.title: Context can change the classification
sessions.translation: A sale on credit · because of hostility.
sessions.prompt: What does an exception or alternative concern teach?
answers: The category has conditions and competing values that must be read in context.
Any exception proves that the original rule was never meaningful.
The exception gives a universal modern permission without further study.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Exceptions reveal the boundaries and purposes of a legal category.

sessions.title: Historical law is not a license for present-day othering
sessions.ref: Jewish Learning Academy Avodah Zarah boundary
sessions.translation: To learn · to distinguish · not to stereotype.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy's responsible stance?
answers: Study the ancient legal categories and their history without assigning a present-day status to a group or neighbor.
Use the tractate as a shortcut for judging contemporary people.
Avoid the tractate because difficult history cannot be examined carefully.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning preserves historical specificity while refusing to turn it into modern stereotyping.

sessions.title: Map a boundary rule in a new source
sessions.translation: Time · action · reason · context.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for an unfamiliar boundary rule?
answers: Name its time, action, stated reason, exceptions, and historical setting before drawing a modern conclusion.
Choose a present-day verdict before reading the source's categories.
Treat every boundary as a claim about the worth of the people involved.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a difficult boundary source with precision, context, and moral seriousness.

bava-batra.pageTitle: Jewish Learning Academy · Bava Batra Arc
bava-batra.kicker: NEZIKIN SOURCE TRAIL · SHARED SPACE AND OBLIGATION
bava-batra.title: Read a shared space through the obligation it creates.
bava-batra.intro: Bava Batra begins with partners who want to divide a courtyard. Map the shared arrangement, the physical detail, the Gemara’s concern about sight, and the measure that answers it.

sessions.title: Partners want to divide a courtyard
sessions.translation: Partners who wished to make a partition in a courtyard.
sessions.prompt: What must be clear before a learner looks for an outcome?
answers: The parties share a space and want to alter its arrangement.
One owner is building alone on private land.
A court has already assigned responsibility for a theft.
sessions.feedback: Right. Start with the people, their shared setting, and the change they seek.

sessions.title: The wall stands in the middle
sessions.translation: They build the wall in the middle.
sessions.prompt: What does this physical detail suggest?
answers: The shared obligation is expressed in a result that does not favor one partner’s side.
The first partner to request a wall becomes its sole owner.
The location has no connection to the source’s reasoning.
sessions.feedback: Good. Legal reasoning can be carried by a concrete spatial detail.

sessions.title: Can sight itself be harm?
sessions.translation: Damage of sight is called damage.
sessions.prompt: What kind of question is this line raising?
answers: Whether loss of privacy can count as a legally meaningful harm.
Whether a wall can be made from physical material.
Whether partners may ever own a courtyard together.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara focuses the case by naming the concern behind the partition.

sessions.title: Four cubits answers the sightline
sessions.translation: Four cubits.
sessions.prompt: How should a reader understand the stated height?
answers: As a measure designed to answer the source’s concern about being seen.
As a round number unrelated to the case’s reason.
As proof that one partner’s property has become more valuable.
sessions.feedback: Right. The source links a concrete measure to the problem it is trying to solve.

sessions.title: Arrangement, request, obligation, reason
sessions.translation: Partnership · request · obligation · harm.
sessions.prompt: Which sequence best preserves the source’s structure?
answers: Shared arrangement, request, obligation, then the reason that makes the obligation intelligible.
A wall height, a court ruling, then a guess about who owns the land.
A privacy concern with no parties or shared arrangement to map.
sessions.feedback: Good. Keep the case and its reason connected rather than treating either as a free-floating fact.

sessions.title: Read a shared-property source
sessions.translation: Who · what · obligation · reason.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first approach to a new shared-property source?
answers: Map the parties and space, name the obligation, then ask which stated concern explains it.
Choose the more sympathetic party before reading the arrangement.
Treat a practical measure as meaningful without looking for its reason.
sessions.feedback: You can now bring a case-map habit into a new civil source without turning it into personal advice.

bava-kamma.pageTitle: Jewish Learning Academy · Bava Kamma Arc
bava-kamma.title: Read a legal world built from categories of damage.
bava-kamma.intro: Bava Kamma teaches a different kind of Gemara reading from Bava Metzia: instead of two symmetrical claims, a Mishnah opens by sorting the world into categories, differentiating each from the others, then asking what they share.

sessions.title: A number opens a legal field
sessions.hebrew: אַרְבָּעָה אָבוֹת נְזִיקִין: הַשּׁוֹר וְהַבּוֹר וְהַמַּבְעֶה וְהַהֶבְעֵר
sessions.translation: There are four primary categories of damage: the ox, the pit, the maveh, and the fire.
sessions.prompt: What should this opening make a learner expect?
answers: A structured legal field with categories the Mishnah will differentiate and compare.
Four independent rulings, one per damager, each needing no comparison.
A dispute among sages over how many primary categories there really are.
sessions.feedback: A numbered, named opening signals a legal field organized by category. The counting question is real — the Gemara later meets teachings that count thirteen and more — but this Mishnah presents structure, not dispute.

sessions.title: Why call it an “av”?
sessions.translation: Fathers / primary categories.
sessions.prompt: Why might the Mishnah call these four categories “avot,” fathers?
answers: The word signals that each is a root category with its own family of derivative cases.
The word ranks the four from the most severe form of damage to the least.
The word honors the early sages in whose names the categories were taught.
sessions.feedback: Calling something an “av” (primary category) invites the question of its “toldot,” derivatives — a structural move that recurs across Shas. It is genealogy of cases, not a severity ranking or an attribution.

sessions.title: Not one is like another
sessions.translation: The ox is not like the maveh.
sessions.prompt: Why would the Mishnah spend its opening lines saying what each category is not?
answers: Because each category needs its own defining feature before any can be grouped together.
Because each difference between categories dictates a different payment for the damage.
Because the Torah listed them separately, and the Mishnah may not merge what Scripture divides.
sessions.feedback: Differentiating first is a real Mishnaic move: the lo-harei lines build toward the shared side, showing no one category could generate the others — they are not a payment schedule or a claim about Scripture’s divisions.

sessions.title: After the differences, a common thread
sessions.hebrew: הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה שֶׁבָּהֶן שֶׁדַּרְכָּן לְהַזִּיק וּשְׁמִירָתָן עָלֶיךָ
sessions.translation: What they share: it is their nature to cause damage, and guarding them is your responsibility.
sessions.prompt: What is the Mishnah doing after four lines of differentiation?
answers: Naming the single principle that lets all four categories share one legal consequence.
Selecting the strongest of the four categories as the model for judging the rest.
Deriving a fifth, broader category from the overlap of the original four.
sessions.feedback: Differentiate, then unify: the tzad hashaveh names what stays constant across all four — it neither crowns one category as the model nor creates a new fifth.

sessions.title: If they share a principle, why not one category?
sessions.translation: Primary category … derivative.
sessions.prompt: If all four categories lead to the same liability, why does the Mishnah insist on keeping them separate?
answers: Because a case that fits two primary categories at once is judged differently than one that fits a category and its own derivative.
Because each of the four requires a different standard of guarding from its owner.
Because merging them would erase the Torah verses in which each appears.
sessions.feedback: The av/toldot structure has real teeth: how a case is counted — two avot versus an av with its toldah — changes the analysis. Guarding standards and source-verses are nearby questions, not this one.

sessions.title: Where do these four categories come from?
sessions.translation: Ox … pit … grazed … kindled.
sessions.prompt: What should a learner expect from the Torah passages behind these four categories?
answers: Separate cases in Exodus that the Mishnah later organizes into one shared legal structure.
A single verse in which all four categories appear together as one law.
Narratives about damage from which the sages inferred general legal rules.
sessions.feedback: Exodus 21–22 gives separate legal cases — a goring ox, an open pit, grazing, spreading fire. They are laws, not stories, and they arrive scattered; the Mishnah’s achievement is the structure.

sessions.title: Claims still need a category first
sessions.translation: Two people are holding a garment.
sessions.prompt: You already learned to weigh competing claims in Bava Metzia. What has to happen before a Bava Kamma claim can even be weighed?
answers: The case must first be sorted into the right category of damage, since the category determines what counts as evidence.
The claims must be weighed first, since evidence questions always precede category questions.
A court must be convened, since damages require judges while found objects do not.
sessions.feedback: Civil law needs both moves in the right order: in damages, the category shapes what evidence even matters — the inverse order is exactly the tempting mistake.

sessions.title: Categories are not a verdict
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: You can now name the four categories of damage. What is Jewish Learning Academy’s appropriate role from here?
answers: Help learners trace the categories and their reasoning while directing any real liability question to qualified guidance.
Let a learner decide a real damages dispute using these four categories alone.
Avoid teaching the categories to prevent any practical questions from arising.
sessions.feedback: Real damages cases turn on facts, intent, and context far beyond four category names — that always needs a qualified authority, not a beginner’s course.

sessions.title: Map the field on your own
sessions.hebrew: אַרְבָּעָה אָבוֹת · לֹא הֲרֵי הַשּׁוֹר כַּהֲרֵי הַמַּבְעֶה · הַצַּד הַשָּׁוֶה
sessions.translation: Four primary categories · the ox is not like the maveh · what they share.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move with this Mishnah?
answers: Name the categories, track how each is differentiated, then find the principle that unifies them.
Find the Torah verse behind each category before reading the Mishnah further.
Begin from the shared principle and reason back to why four categories exist.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a categories-and-principle sugya with a concrete map — verse-hunting and principle-first reading are real approaches, but they invert the Mishnah’s own order.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: Fathers / primary categories.
sessions.prompt: What does avot signal in this Mishnah?
answers: Primary categories from which related cases can be understood.
The names of the first teachers of the tractate.
A category that closes the discussion.
sessions.feedback: You can recognize a root category and distinguish it from an attribution or a closing marker.

bava-metzia.pageTitle: Jewish Learning Academy · Bava Metzia Arc
bava-metzia.title: Read a legal world built from civil dispute.
bava-metzia.intro: Bava Metzia teaches a different kind of Gemara reading: two symmetrical claims, a Mishnah response that has to be justified, and evidence that must be weighed rather than assumed.

sessions.title: Two people, one object
sessions.translation: Two people are holding a garment.
sessions.prompt: What basic situation does the Mishnah place before the reader?
answers: Two people make competing claims over the same object.
Two partners disagree about how to divide shared property.
A finder and an owner dispute whether an object was abandoned.
sessions.feedback: Correct. Start with the human and legal conflict before parsing the remedies — this is not a partnership dissolving or an abandonment question, though both live nearby in the tractate.

sessions.title: Why an ordinary object?
sessions.translation: Garment.
sessions.prompt: Why does a civil-law Mishnah often open with a specific, ordinary object like this?
answers: A concrete object lets the Mishnah test general principles of claims and evidence against a real case.
A garment has halakhic properties that make this dispute unique to clothing.
The case is historical: a real garment dispute the court once decided.
sessions.feedback: Right. Civil law becomes intelligible through a concrete case — the garment is an example carrying general principles, not a clothing-specific rule or a court record.

sessions.title: Each person says: I found it
sessions.hebrew: זה אומר אני מצאתיה וזה אומר אני מצאתיה
sessions.translation: This one says, “I found it,” and this one says, “I found it.”
sessions.prompt: Why does the Mishnah repeat the identical claim from both sides?
answers: It establishes that neither side’s assertion alone settles the dispute.
It shows that at least one of the two claimants must be lying.
It signals that the finder’s claim is weaker than an owner’s would be.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Parallel claims create the evidentiary problem the Mishnah must address — the Gemara itself will ask whether both could be honest, so “someone is lying” is exactly the shortcut to resist.

sessions.title: What must the court decide?
sessions.translation: They divide [it].
sessions.prompt: Before treating this short ruling as simple, what should a learner ask?
answers: What facts, claims, and legal principles make this response appropriate?
Whether dividing is meant literally or as a payment of half the value.
Why the court does not simply award the garment to the first claimant.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara’s work is to test how and why a terse Mishnah response follows from its case — the narrower questions about mechanics and alternatives live inside that larger one.

sessions.title: When would the answer differ?
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: Why might a later Gemara ask for the reason behind “they divide it,” instead of accepting it as obviously fair?
answers: The reasoning determines whether the same solution applies when the claims or evidence are not perfectly symmetrical.
A ruling without a stated reason cannot be relied upon in practice.
Fairness is not a category the Gemara accepts as a legal argument.
sessions.feedback: Right. A stated reason lets a ruling travel responsibly to a case that is not perfectly symmetrical — the Gemara asks why in order to map the ruling’s reach, not to discredit it.

sessions.title: Evidence must be tested
sessions.translation: Come and hear.
sessions.prompt: If a source were brought here to test the fairness of dividing the garment, what should a learner do with it?
answers: Test whether the cited source actually supports or complicates the question under discussion.
Check whether the source is a Mishnah or a baraita before weighing it.
Ask which sage transmitted the source and how reliable he was.
sessions.feedback: Good. A source is not self-explanatory; its role in the argument must be read first — genre and attribution matter later, but function comes before pedigree.

sessions.title: Track what each move contributes
sessions.translation: Question · answer · sign · proof.
sessions.prompt: This argument map comes from Berakhot. What should carry over into a civil-law case like this one?
answers: Track what each piece of evidence contributes before deciding whether a claim is secure.
Expect the same sequence — question, answer, sign, proof — in the same order here.
Reuse the Berakhot conclusions, since the method validated them there.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The habit transfers; the specific sequence and the old conclusions do not — that is the difference between carrying a skill and carrying an answer.

sessions.title: Map the case on your own
sessions.hebrew: שְׁנַיִם אוֹחֲזִין בְּטַלִּית · זה אומר אני מצאתיה · יחלוקו
sessions.translation: Two people are holding a garment · this one says, “I found it” · they divide it.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move with an unfamiliar civil-law case like this?
answers: Identify who is involved, what each side claims, and what response the Mishnah gives, before asking why.
Ask why the court divides the object, since the reason unlocks the case.
Compare this case with the closest parallel case you already know.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a claims-and-evidence sugya with a concrete map — the why-question and the parallel-hunt are strong second moves, but the map comes first.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: They divide [it].
sessions.prompt: What response does this word name?
answers: They divide it.
They dismiss the claim.
They bring a verse as proof.
sessions.feedback: You can identify the Mishnah’s response and distinguish it from a dismissal or proof-text move.

beitzah.kicker: MOED SOURCE TRAIL · CASE, CATEGORY, REASON
beitzah.title: Read a dispute through the category beneath it.
beitzah.intro: Beitzah begins with an egg laid on a festival. Map the shared case, preserve Hillel and Shammai, then ask why different explanations of one ruling matter.

sessions.title: An egg appears during the festival
sessions.translation: An egg that was laid on a festival day.
sessions.prompt: What fact is the source putting under pressure?
answers: The egg came into being during the festival rather than beforehand.
The egg was prepared before the festival and stored away.
The source is telling a story with no legal category to map.
sessions.feedback: Right. Timing is the case fact that makes the category question possible.

sessions.title: Shammai and Hillel disagree
sessions.hebrew: בֵּית שַׁמַּאי אוֹמְרִים תֵּאָכֵל · בֵּית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים לֹא תֵּאָכֵל
sessions.translation: Beit Shammai say it may be eaten; Beit Hillel say it may not.
sessions.prompt: What must a reader preserve first?
answers: Two answers to the same case before deciding why they differ.
That the longer wording automatically wins.
That the two schools are talking about unrelated cases.
sessions.feedback: Good. Map each voice before importing an explanation.

sessions.title: Nolad: newly come into being
sessions.translation: Newly come into being.
sessions.prompt: What does naming nolad allow the learner to do?
answers: See the egg as one instance of a category rather than an isolated curiosity.
Treat the Hebrew term as a final ruling by itself.
Assume every new object is identical in every legal setting.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Categories make a specific case portable without erasing further distinctions.

sessions.title: A category is not a shortcut
sessions.translation: Newly come into being · a case.
sessions.prompt: After identifying a category, what does a careful reader still need to ask?
answers: Which facts of this case make the category relevant here.
Whether the category ends all further questions.
Which school has the more memorable name.
sessions.feedback: Yes. A category organizes a case; it does not replace attending to the facts.

sessions.title: Two reasons, one prohibition
sessions.translation: Because of preparation · because of a newly-created thing.
sessions.prompt: Why does the Gemara test more than one reason for the same ruling?
answers: Different reasons can change which further cases the ruling reaches.
A ruling is invalid until two reasons are found.
The Gemara has abandoned the original case.
sessions.feedback: Right. A disagreement about reason can reshape the scope of an agreed ruling.

sessions.title: Reason controls the next question
sessions.translation: Reason · a practical difference.
sessions.prompt: What should a reader look for after two reasons are proposed?
answers: A later case where the reasons would lead to different outcomes.
A way to ignore the original disagreement.
A reason to merge two distinct explanations.
sessions.feedback: Good. Testing a reason means asking what difference it would make in another case.

sessions.title: Study is not a personal ruling
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of this source?
answers: Learn its categories and seek qualified guidance for practical observance.
Apply the source directly to a personal holiday question.
Ignore the source’s practical stakes completely.
sessions.feedback: Serious study includes recognizing its boundary.

sessions.title: Read a new category dispute
sessions.translation: Case · category · voice · reason.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new dispute?
answers: State the case, preserve each voice, name the category, then test the reason’s scope.
Choose the familiar voice before reading the case.
Treat a category word as an answer without looking at reasons.
sessions.feedback: You can now follow case, category, and reason without flattening the dispute.

bekhorot.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · STATUS, OWNERSHIP, REDEMPTION
bekhorot.title: Read how a firstborn status changes with facts, categories, and conditions.
bekhorot.intro: Bekhorot asks how birth, ownership, domain, sanctity, and redemption fit together. Follow the case before deciding what consequence follows.

sessions.title: A firstborn in changing hands
sessions.translation: firstborn animal · domain · sanctity
sessions.prompt: What pressure does the opening case create?
answers: It asks how ownership and place affect the status of a firstborn animal.
It treats the animal as ordinary property in every setting because a change of owner cannot alter a status that began at birth.
It treats sanctity as a private feeling rather than a source-defined category, so domain and birth details can be left aside.
sessions.feedback: Right. The case makes status depend on facts about ownership, birth, and domain.

sessions.title: Status before remedy
sessions.translation: firstborn · consecrated things
sessions.prompt: What should a reader identify before asking what happens next?
answers: Whether the animal is in the firstborn category at all.
Whether every firstborn should be treated as ordinary property until someone performs a later act, without first asking whether the category attaches.
Whether the source has no legal categories and is merely describing a custom rather than a status with consequences.
sessions.feedback: Good. First identify the status; only then can you ask about ownership, sanctity, or redemption.

sessions.title: Who owns the animal?
sessions.translation: Israelite domain · non-Jewish domain
sessions.prompt: Why does the source track whose domain the animal is in?
answers: The ownership fact may determine whether the firstborn obligation attaches.
Ownership never changes a legal analysis, because once the animal is born its later domain cannot affect which obligations the source describes.
The domain is included only as narrative decoration, a setting detail that should not shape the legal category or its consequences.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A legal reading preserves the factual trigger instead of treating the animal as context-free.

sessions.title: Status is not yet redemption
sessions.translation: sanctity · redemption
sessions.prompt: What distinction should remain visible?
answers: An animal can have a status, while redemption is a separate legal move with its own conditions.
Sanctity and redemption always mean the same thing, so naming an animal status already tells us that the later remedy has occurred.
Redemption erases the need to identify the original status, because the final transfer is the only legally meaningful moment.
sessions.feedback: Right. The map keeps the initial status distinct from the later remedy or transfer.

sessions.title: Why does the fact matter?
sessions.translation: What is the reason? · From where?
sessions.prompt: What does a Gemara reason-question invite here?
answers: Ask what principle makes ownership or birth-location legally decisive.
Pick the most familiar ritual practice and treat its customary shape as the explanation, even if the fact pattern points to a different legal concern.
Ignore the Mishnah factual wording and look only for a general religious principle, since the concrete case cannot explain the rule.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Gemara turns the case into a question about the rule beneath the fact pattern.

sessions.title: Find the limiting condition
sessions.translation: condition · uncertainty · limiting term
sessions.prompt: What should a reader test after finding the rule?
answers: Which condition changes the status and which nearby facts leave it intact.
Whether one condition must control every case, even when the source introduces a different ownership, birth, or uncertainty fact that could change the result.
Whether the source can be read without separating cases, because every nearby detail is merely an illustration of one broad rule.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Scope work asks exactly where the rule applies and where a condition limits it.

sessions.title: Historical sanctity categories
sessions.translation: to learn · to understand · to ask
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of these firstborn and sanctity sources?
answers: Study their categories and reasoning as historical textual literacy.
Treat the lesson as current practical ritual guidance.
Avoid the legal reasoning because the Temple setting is historical.
sessions.feedback: Serious study can honor the source while clearly distinguishing historical categories from practical guidance.

sessions.title: Map status before remedy
sessions.translation: status · fact · consequence · limit
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new firstborn case?
answers: State the status, identify the decisive fact, name the consequence, then test the limit.
Choose a remedy before identifying the animal’s status.
Treat ownership, sanctity, and redemption as interchangeable.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a Bekhorot case by tracking status, facts, consequences, and limits in order.

berakhot.kicker: BERAKHOT · FROM FIRST WORDS TO FIRST SUGYA
berakhot.title: A real path through the opening of Shas.
berakhot.intro: Berakhot is not a collection of screens. It is a sequence: learn the signals, enter a Mishnah, follow a question, weigh evidence, read a disagreement, retrieve fragile skills, then meet an unfamiliar passage on your own.

outcome.heading: Read a short opening sugya with a map.
outcome.body: By the end, a learner can name the case, identify the question, follow an answer and proof, recognize disagreement, and use translation to verify rather than replace reading.

sessions.title: Core Gemara signals
sessions.copy: Twelve high-frequency words that tell you what the page is doing.

sessions.title: Enter Berakhot 2a
sessions.copy: Find the Mishnah, the context-question, and the verse-based answer.

sessions.title: Build a proof
sessions.copy: Follow a word-question, answer, sign, and second source on Berakhot 2b.

sessions.title: Transfer the moves
sessions.copy: Read unfamiliar Berakhot signals with translation used only to verify.

sessions.title: Read Mishnah grammar
sessions.copy: Use compact Hebrew structure to separate case, condition, and ruling.

sessions.title: Follow a cited teaching
sessions.copy: Track baraita, objection, and response without losing the thread.

sessions.title: Gemara argument toolkit
sessions.copy: Practice connectors, objections, distinctions, and conclusions across contexts.

sessions.title: Retrieval session
sessions.copy: Bring back fragile source moves before beginning new material.

sessions.title: Independent reading
sessions.copy: Meet unfamiliar Gemara signals without the scaffold.

sessions.title: Launch into a new tractate
sessions.copy: Use your Berakhot tools in Eruvin, Shabbat, Pesachim, or Bava Metzia.

sessions.title: Begin with desire
sessions.translation: One thing I ask of the Lord.
sessions.prompt: What inner question can this verse open?
answers: What it means for a life to be oriented by a deepest desire.
Which claimant owns an object.
Which category of damages applies.
sessions.feedback: Good. Chassidic reading begins from the source’s language about inner orientation.

sessions.title: A metaphor carries an idea
sessions.translation: The human soul is the lamp of the Lord.
sessions.prompt: What should a learner ask of this metaphor?
answers: What qualities of a lamp illuminate the source’s account of the soul.
Which legal code settles the verse.
How to avoid interpreting imagery.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Metaphor is not decoration; it is a conceptual tool.

sessions.title: Intention joins action
sessions.translation: Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one.
sessions.prompt: How can a Chassidic reader extend this source responsibly?
answers: Ask how attention and intention can deepen a practice without changing its legal form.
Replace practice with emotion alone.
Treat reflection as a personal ruling.
sessions.feedback: Right. Inner work can illuminate practice without displacing halakhic reasoning.

sessions.title: One source, more than one emphasis
sessions.translation: Joy · awe.
sessions.prompt: What is a fair comparative question?
answers: How might different Chassidic sources balance joy and awe in service?
Which concept makes the other unnecessary?
Why compare sources at all?
sessions.feedback: Good. Comparison preserves distinct emphases rather than flattening a tradition.

sessions.title: Text before projection
sessions.translation: Source · concept · implication.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible order of learning?
answers: Read the source, define its concept, then consider a possible implication.
Begin with a feeling and make the source agree.
Skip the text for a personal slogan.
sessions.feedback: This keeps inner learning anchored in the text.

sessions.title: Ask a source-grounded question
sessions.translation: To behold the pleasantness of the Lord.
sessions.prompt: What is a source-grounded next question?
answers: How does the verse describe the relationship between attention, beauty, and divine service?
Which sentence is easiest to memorize?
What ruling should every person follow?
sessions.feedback: You can now use a source to open a careful inner question.

chagigah.kicker: MOED SOURCE TRAIL · SCOPE, EXCEPTION, CAREFUL READING
chagigah.title: Read a sweeping rule without losing its limits—or its historical setting.
chagigah.intro: Chagigah opens with a broad pilgrimage obligation and a list of exceptions. Learn to map the rule, notice what the Gemara asks about its scope, and read historical legal classifications with care.

sessions.title: A sweeping obligation
sessions.translation: All are obligated in the appearance offering.
sessions.prompt: What should a reader notice first about this opening?
answers: It begins with a broad claim before giving its qualifications.
It states a rule limited to one named individual.
It offers a narrative without a legal structure.
sessions.feedback: Right. A sweeping opening gives the reader a scope claim to test against what follows.

sessions.title: The rule is immediately qualified
sessions.translation: Except from.
sessions.prompt: What is the first reading move when a source follows “all” with “except”?
answers: Keep both the broad rule and the stated qualification visible.
Assume the exception makes the broad rule meaningless.
Ignore the exception because the opening is more memorable.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The structure is rule plus limit; neither line may erase the other.

sessions.title: A historical classification is not a timeless verdict
sessions.translation: Exempt.
sessions.prompt: How should a modern learner approach the source’s ancient classifications?
answers: Read their legal function and historical setting without treating them as judgments of human worth.
Repeat the categories as if they directly settle modern questions.
Skip the source because historical language cannot be studied.
sessions.feedback: Good. Careful study neither erases difficult language nor turns it into a contemporary verdict.

sessions.title: What does “all” really mean?
sessions.translation: “All” comes to include what?
sessions.prompt: What does the Gemara’s question about “all” ask the reader to do?
answers: Test the exact scope of the Mishnah’s broad wording.
Replace the Mishnah with an unrelated topic.
Treat the opening word as too obvious to examine.
sessions.feedback: Right. A compact universal word can carry a question about inclusion and scope.

sessions.title: Inclusion is not endorsement
sessions.translation: General rule · particular case.
sessions.prompt: Why separate the scope question from a moral judgment about the source?
answers: The Gemara’s reading question and a modern ethical evaluation are related but not identical tasks.
A scope question automatically resolves every modern ethical concern.
Historical context makes close reading unnecessary.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Responsible learning names which question a source is answering and which question we bring to it.

sessions.title: An exception does work
sessions.translation: Obligation · exemption.
sessions.prompt: What does an explicit exception reveal about the opening obligation?
answers: It shows that the source is defining the scope of its legal category.
It proves that categories are not used in legal texts.
It makes the opening statement irrelevant.
sessions.feedback: Good. Exceptions help the reader see the boundary the legal category is drawing.

sessions.title: Study is not personal classification
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy’s responsible role with this source?
answers: Support careful historical study without assigning anyone a present-day status or obligation.
Use the Mishnah to classify a learner’s own religious standing.
Avoid the text because its setting differs from ours.
sessions.feedback: Serious study includes refusing to turn an ancient classification into a personal ruling.

sessions.title: Map a new universal claim
sessions.translation: Rule · exception · context.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a source that begins with a universal claim and then qualifies it?
answers: State the rule, mark the exception, test the wording, then read the setting.
Choose a personal outcome before examining the source.
Treat the exception as a reason to ignore the rule.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a broad claim through both its textual limits and its historical context.

chassidus.kicker: CHASSIDUS ARC · JOY, AWE, AND INTENTION
chassidus.title: Hold two inner postures together.
chassidus.intro: Chassidic reading does not resolve joy and awe into one another. It reads a source-grounded desire, a metaphor for the soul, and a call to careful practice, and asks how each posture shapes the others.

sessions.title: Begin with a single desire
sessions.translation: One thing I ask of the Lord.
sessions.prompt: What inner question does this verse open for a Chassidic reader?
answers: What it means for a life to be oriented by a single deepest desire.
Which claimant owns an object.
Which category of damages applies.
sessions.feedback: Good. Chassidic reading begins from the source’s language about inner orientation.

sessions.title: Not opposites, but a pair
sessions.hebrew: עִבְדוּ אֶת ה׳ בְּיִרְאָה וְגִילוּ בִּרְעָדָה
sessions.translation: Serve the Lord with awe, and rejoice with trembling.
sessions.prompt: What interpretive question is most useful for this pairing?
answers: How joy and awe may be held together rather than treated as opposites.
Which emotion removes the need for practice.
Which word is easiest to memorize.
sessions.feedback: Right. Chassidic sources often hold two postures in tension rather than resolving one into the other.

sessions.title: A metaphor carries an idea
sessions.translation: The human soul is the lamp of the Lord.
sessions.prompt: What should a learner ask of this metaphor?
answers: What qualities of a lamp illuminate the source’s account of the soul.
Which legal code settles the verse.
How to avoid interpreting imagery.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Metaphor is not decoration; it is a conceptual tool.

sessions.title: Joy and awe reach into action
sessions.translation: Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one.
sessions.prompt: How can joy and awe extend this teaching about small and large practice?
answers: Ask how attention, joy, and awe can deepen a practice without changing its legal form.
Replace practice with emotion alone.
Treat reflection as a personal ruling.
sessions.feedback: Right. Inner posture can illuminate practice without displacing halakhic reasoning.

sessions.title: Text before projection
sessions.translation: Source · concept · implication.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible order of learning here?
answers: Read the source, define its concept, then consider a possible implication.
Begin with a feeling and make the source agree.
Skip the text for a personal slogan.
sessions.feedback: This keeps inner learning anchored in the text.

sessions.title: What the desire is actually for
sessions.translation: To behold the pleasantness of the Lord.
sessions.prompt: How does this phrase extend the desire named in step one?
answers: It names what the single desire is actually oriented toward: beholding pleasantness, not merely wanting.
It cancels the earlier desire entirely.
It has no relationship to the earlier verse.
sessions.feedback: Good. A verse can extend and specify an idea introduced earlier in the same passage.

sessions.title: A Mussar source, a Chassidic question
sessions.translation: The shy person does not learn.
sessions.prompt: This source comes from Mussar study. What question does it also raise for joy and awe?
answers: Whether awe can tip into a hesitation that blocks the courage joy requires.
Whether shyness is unrelated to religious life.
Whether Mussar and Chassidus never share any concerns.
sessions.feedback: The same source can open related questions across different subjects.

sessions.title: Map the inner posture on your own
sessions.translation: One thing I ask · joy · awe.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move across these three fragments?
answers: Name the desire, then ask how joy and awe each shape the way that desire is pursued.
Pick whichever fragment feels most comforting.
Assume the three fragments are unrelated.
sessions.feedback: You can now hold desire, joy, and awe together as one connected reading question.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: One thing I ask of the Lord.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase in a few words.
acceptable: one thing i ask of the lord
one thing i have asked of the lord
one thing i ask from the lord
one thing have i asked of the lord
one thing i ask of god
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

chullin.kicker: A RULE READ THROUGH ITS EXCEPTION
chullin.title: Read a broad rule by tracing what narrows it.
chullin.intro: Chullin opens with the widest possible rule — everyone may slaughter — then immediately narrows it. The exception, its reason, and the condition that reopens it are where the real legal reasoning lives.

sessions.title: A broad rule opens the tractate
sessions.translation: All may slaughter, and their slaughter is valid.
sessions.prompt: What does the Mishnah state before listing any qualifications or exceptions?
answers: A broad statement about who may validly perform an action.
A story about a festival.
A measure of a courtyard.
sessions.feedback: Good. First locate the scope of the statement — the exceptions have not appeared yet.

sessions.title: A general word creates work
sessions.translation: All.
sessions.prompt: What should a careful Gemara reader ask when seeing “all”?
answers: Who is really included, and whether any exceptions are about to qualify it.
What page comes next.
Which word is a verse.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. General language like “all” often becomes the focus of a close Gemara analysis.

sessions.title: The rule immediately narrows
sessions.translation: Except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor.
sessions.prompt: What does naming these three exceptions do to the opening rule?
answers: It narrows “all” to exclude three specific categories of people from validly performing the act on their own.
It cancels the rule completely.
It adds three more people who may always slaughter.
sessions.feedback: Right. A sweeping rule is almost never left unqualified — the exception clause is where the real legal content often lives.

sessions.title: The exception has its own reason
sessions.translation: Lest they spoil it.
sessions.prompt: What kind of concern does this phrase reveal about why these three are excluded?
answers: A concern about competence and reliability in performing the act correctly, not a personal judgment about their worth.
A concern that has nothing to do with the act of slaughter itself.
A concern that applies equally to every person, with no exceptions at all.
sessions.feedback: Good. “Lest they spoil it” names a functional worry about reliable performance — this is what makes the exception a legal category, not a label.

sessions.title: The same rule, one condition later
sessions.hebrew: וְכֻלָּן שֶׁשָּׁחֲטוּ וַאֲחֵרִים רוֹאִין אוֹתָן שְׁחִיטָתָן כְּשֵׁרָה
sessions.translation: But if any of them slaughtered while others were watching, their slaughter is valid.
sessions.prompt: What does this final clause reveal about the true concern behind the exception?
answers: The concern was reliable performance, not fixed personal status — supervision by others resolves it without changing who the person is.
The exception clause was a mistake that this line simply erases.
Supervision has no legal effect at all.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Mishnah names a concern, then shows a condition that satisfies that same concern — a pattern worth recognizing across Shas.

sessions.title: Rule, exception, condition
sessions.translation: A rule · what departs from the rule · a condition.
sessions.prompt: Which sequence describes the structure you just traced?
answers: A broad rule, a narrowing exception, and a condition that reopens the rule for the excluded cases.
A final ruling stated once with no discussion.
Three unrelated statements placed next to each other by accident.
sessions.feedback: This three-part shape — rule, exception, condition — recurs across many opening Mishnayot.

sessions.title: Kashrut needs a qualified authority
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: How should a learner treat this source about a practical, halakhically consequential activity?
answers: Study its structure and reasoning carefully while recognizing that any real kashrut question needs a qualified authority, not this course.
Treat the Mishnah as sufficient personal guidance for a real question about kosher slaughter.
Avoid the topic because it concerns practical law.
sessions.feedback: Right. Source literacy includes knowing exactly where study ends and a real practical question begins.

sessions.title: A fixed detail concealed a reason before
sessions.hebrew: בָּתֵּי דִינִין יוֹשְׁבִין בָּעֲיָירוֹת בַּשֵּׁנִי וּבַחֲמִישִׁי
sessions.translation: Courts sit in the towns on Monday and Thursday.
sessions.prompt: You already learned that Ketubot’s Wednesday schedule concealed an institutional reason. What does that habit add to reading Chullin’s exception clause?
answers: A rule or an exception is rarely arbitrary — asking what functional concern it serves often uncovers a condition that can satisfy that same concern.
That every legal detail is decorative and has no underlying reason.
That reasons behind rules can never be recovered from the text.
sessions.feedback: The same discipline — ask what concern a detail serves — reads a wedding schedule and a slaughtering exception with the same care.

sessions.title: Map the rule on your own
sessions.hebrew: הַכֹּל שׁוֹחֲטִין · חוּץ מֵחֵרֵשׁ שׁוֹטֶה וְקָטָן · שֶׁמָּא יְקַלְקְלוּ
sessions.translation: All may slaughter · except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor · lest they spoil it.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move across these three fragments?
answers: Name the broad rule, find its exception, then ask what concern the exception is protecting against.
Assume the rule applies with no exceptions.
Memorize the English without tracking the Hebrew structure.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a rule-and-exception sugya with a concrete map.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: Lest they spoil it / ruin it.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase in a few words.
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

chumash.kicker: TORAH ARC · SHEMA AND ITS RECEPTION
chumash.title: Read a verse before reading what later texts do with it.
chumash.intro: This arc begins with Deuteronomy’s Shema passage, learns to see command, setting, repetition, and ambiguity, then traces how Mishnah and Gemara receive its language.

sessions.title: Name the address
sessions.hebrew: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד
sessions.translation: Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one.
sessions.prompt: What is the first close-reading task?
answers: Identify who is addressed and what claim the verse makes.
Identify how the verse is used in the daily prayer service.
Identify which of the verse’s words carry legal obligations.
sessions.feedback: Good. Start with speaker, audience, and the claim — liturgical use and legal weight are real questions, but they are reception, and reception comes after reading.

sessions.title: What is the person asked to do?
sessions.translation: You shall love the Lord your God.
sessions.prompt: What kind of statement is this?
answers: A command that names a relationship and orientation.
A promise describing a reward that will follow obedience.
A declaration reporting what Israel already feels.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The vav-consecutive form commands — it neither promises nor describes, though both readings tempt because love sounds like feeling rather than obligation.

sessions.title: A word appears across settings
sessions.translation: You shall speak of them.
sessions.prompt: What should a close reader ask next?
answers: Where and when does the verse say this speaking should take place?
What content do “them” — the words — actually contain?
Why does the verse choose speech over silent remembering?
sessions.feedback: A repeated or extended instruction often carries its meaning through the details that follow — and the verse does immediately supply settings, so follow where it leads.

sessions.title: Two times frame the instruction
sessions.translation: When you lie down and when you rise up.
sessions.prompt: What does this phrase first contribute inside the verse?
answers: It places the instruction in the rhythms of daily life.
It fixes two halakhic times at which recitation is required.
It restricts the instruction to the home, excluding the road.
sessions.feedback: Right. First read the phrase in its verse — the fixed-times reading is exactly what the Mishnah will later build, but the verse itself speaks the language of daily rhythm.

sessions.title: One phrase, more than one possible focus
sessions.translation: When you lie down and when you rise up.
sessions.prompt: What is a responsible interpretive question?
answers: Does the phrase describe ordinary life, particular times, or both—and what evidence guides the reading?
Which of the classical commentators offers the most authoritative reading of the phrase?
How did the phrase come to be recited twice daily in the liturgy?
sessions.feedback: Good. Interpretation begins with a precise question grounded in the text — authority-ranking and liturgical history are downstream of first asking what the words can mean.

sessions.title: A later text foregrounds one question
sessions.translation: From when do we recite Shema in the evenings?
sessions.prompt: How does the Mishnah receive the Torah passage?
answers: It turns the daily-language of the verse into a practical timing question.
It quotes the verse and explains each of its words in order.
It expands the verse’s command to cover study as well as recitation.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Canonical reception can highlight one dimension of a verse for a new kind of question — the Mishnah neither glosses word-by-word nor expands; it selects.

sessions.title: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah begins here
sessions.translation: The Mishnah relies on a verse.
sessions.prompt: What does the Gemara add to the Mishnah’s use of the verse?
answers: It explains the textual reason behind the Mishnah’s ordering.
It challenges whether the Mishnah read the verse correctly.
It supplies the clock times the Mishnah left unstated.
sessions.feedback: You can now see Torah, Mishnah, and Gemara as a connected conversation — here the Gemara grounds the Mishnah rather than attacking it or filling in its times.

sessions.title: Trace the source forward
sessions.translation: When you lie down and when you rise up · from when?
sessions.prompt: What relationship should a learner recognize?
answers: The Mishnah’s question and Gemara’s explanation are later readings of language in the Torah verse.
The Torah verse summarizes a practice the Mishnah had already established.
The two texts address the same practice independently, without contact.
sessions.feedback: This is canonical literacy: reading each layer clearly while tracing the line between them — and knowing which direction the line runs.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: When you lie down and when you rise up.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase.
acceptable: when you lie down and when you rise up
when you lie down and rise up
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

eruvin.title: Read a legal world built from measurement.
eruvin.intro: Eruvin teaches a Gemara-reading skill Berakhot and Shabbat only began: physical measurement as the trigger for a legal category, and the reasoning that connects a measure to its purpose.

sessions.title: A measurement opens the case
sessions.hebrew: מָבוֹי שֶׁהוּא גָבוֹהַּ לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה
sessions.translation: An alleyway whose entrance is higher than twenty cubits.
sessions.prompt: What kind of information does this opening give, before any ruling is stated?
answers: A concrete physical measurement that will determine the legal outcome.
A story about the person who built the alleyway.
A final ruling with no case attached.
sessions.feedback: Good. Eruvin often opens with a measurement, not an abstract principle.

sessions.title: Name the shared space
sessions.translation: Alleyway / shared passage.
sessions.prompt: Why does Eruvin spend so much attention on a space like this?
answers: Because shared space raises the boundary questions the tractate is organized around.
Because an alleyway has no legal significance.
Because the word only appears once in the Mishnah.
sessions.feedback: Right. A shared passage sits between fully private and fully public space, which is exactly what Eruvin studies.

sessions.title: A measurement triggers a response
sessions.translation: One should lower it.
sessions.prompt: What must a learner map before treating this as a final answer?
answers: The measurement, the requirement it triggers, and what response the Mishnah gives.
Only the final word, without the case that produced it.
Whether the alleyway has a name.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A short response like this only makes sense attached to the case that required it.

sessions.title: Condition plus response equals category
sessions.translation: An alleyway that is high … one should lower it.
sessions.prompt: Reading the condition and response together, what is the Mishnah organizing?
answers: A category: a physical feature that must be corrected before the space counts as a valid shared domain.
A list of unrelated alleyways.
A prohibition with no stated reason or response.
sessions.feedback: Good. A measure becomes a category once you see what response it requires.

sessions.title: A rule invites a reason
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: Why does a careful reader ask this instead of simply accepting the twenty-cubit rule?
answers: Naming the reason lets a learner tell when the same rule should or should not extend to a new case.
The question is decorative and changes nothing about how the rule applies.
Reasons are never given for measurements in Mishnah.
sessions.feedback: Right. A stated reason is what lets a rule travel responsibly to an unfamiliar case.

sessions.title: The Gemara presses the Mishnah
sessions.translation: Why?
sessions.prompt: This word opens the Gemara’s engagement with the Mishnah. What should a learner expect to follow?
answers: A cited source or line of reasoning that explains why the measurement matters.
The end of the discussion with no further text.
A new, unrelated Mishnah.
sessions.feedback: Good. A bare “why?” is an invitation, not a conclusion — expect the page to answer it.

sessions.short: A new case: kashering the alley
sessions.title: From measurement to physical markers
sessions.translation: Beit Shammai say: a side-post and a crossbeam.
sessions.prompt: After establishing the twenty-cubit measure, what does the very next Mishnah address?
answers: A dispute about what physical markers make an alleyway valid for carrying.
A repeat of the same measurement rule using different words.
The end of the tractate’s discussion of alleyways entirely.
sessions.feedback: Right. Once a space is identified, the next question is what marks its boundary — a natural continuation, not a repeat.

sessions.title: “And” versus “or”
sessions.hebrew: וּבֵית הִלֵּל אוֹמְרִים לֶחִי אוֹ קוֹרָה
sessions.translation: And Beit Hillel say: a side-post or a crossbeam.
sessions.prompt: What is the structural difference between the two positions?
answers: Beit Shammai requires both markers together; Beit Hillel accepts either one alone.
The two schools agree completely and simply use different words for the same rule.
Beit Hillel requires more physical construction than Beit Shammai.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A single conjunction — “and” versus “or” — is the entire substance of this Tannaitic dispute.

sessions.title: The same measurement, a new tractate
sessions.hebrew: סֻכָּה שֶׁהִיא גְבוֹהָה לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה
sessions.translation: A sukkah that is higher than twenty cubits.
sessions.prompt: This is the same measurement read in a different tractate. What skill carries over from Eruvin?
answers: Read the concrete measurement first, then ask what legal category it triggers.
Assume every tractate uses the measurement for the same purpose.
Skip the measurement and look for the ruling only.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The habit of reading a measurement before its consequence transfers across tractates.

sessions.title: A measurement is not a ruling
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: You now know the Mishnah’s twenty-cubit measure. What is Jewish Learning Academy’s appropriate role from here?
answers: Help learners trace the source and its reasoning while directing any real-world eruv or carrying question to qualified guidance.
Let a learner determine their own neighborhood’s eruv status from this measurement alone.
Avoid teaching measurements to prevent any practical questions.
sessions.feedback: A number in the Mishnah is a starting point for study, not enough on its own to determine a real eruv’s validity — that always requires a qualified, on-the-ground rabbinic determination.

sessions.title: Map the case on your own
sessions.translation: Alleyway · higher than twenty cubits · one should lower it.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move with this case?
answers: Identify the object, its measurement, and the response the measurement requires.
Guess the ruling from the first word alone.
Assume the case has already been fully explained.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a measurement-based sugya with a concrete map.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: Why?
sessions.prompt: What question does this word ask?
answers: Why?
From when?
Who is obligated?
sessions.feedback: You can recognize this question signal in a new source without needing to produce it from a blank field.

gittin.kicker: NASHIM SOURCE TRAIL - DOCUMENT, AGENCY, DELIVERY
gittin.title: Read how a document becomes a legal act.
gittin.intro: Gittin asks how writing, representation, intent, and delivery work together to create a legally meaningful document. Learn each condition before drawing conclusions.

sessions.title: A get is a defined legal instrument
sessions.translation: A divorce document brought from overseas.
sessions.prompt: What is the opening Mishnah asking you to notice?
answers: The document has a defined legal identity and a delivery problem that must be solved.
Any private note automatically dissolves a marriage.
The messenger can replace the document entirely.
sessions.feedback: Right. Gittin begins by distinguishing a formal instrument from an ordinary message.

sessions.title: Who can speak for the sender?
sessions.translation: The agent testifies about the writing and signatures.
sessions.prompt: Why does the agent matter in this opening case?
answers: The agent supplies a defined procedural testimony that connects the document to its origin.
Any traveler may change the document while carrying it.
The recipient must personally witness the original writing.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Agency is structured: the messenger has a role and a limited statement to make.

sessions.title: Writing and signatures do legal work
sessions.translation: He shall write for her a document of severance.
sessions.prompt: What kind of question should a reader ask about the document?
answers: Which writing, signature, and authorization conditions make the document valid for its purpose.
Whether attractive handwriting makes every document valid.
Whether the document can be replaced by an oral promise.
sessions.feedback: Good. Validity is a source-defined set of conditions, not a matter of appearance.

sessions.title: The document must reach its legal destination
sessions.translation: The document enters her possession.
sessions.prompt: What changes when delivery occurs?
answers: The document moves from the sender’s control into the recipient’s legally recognized possession.
The messenger remains the permanent owner of the document.
Delivery is irrelevant once the document has been written.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Delivery is a legal transition, not merely a change of physical location.

sessions.title: Action and intention must be read together
sessions.translation: For her purpose / for her sake.
sessions.prompt: What does an intent requirement prevent?
answers: It prevents a document or act from being treated as interchangeable when its legally relevant purpose is missing.
It makes the recipient’s intention irrelevant.
It turns every mistaken act into a valid divorce.
sessions.feedback: Right. Gittin trains you to ask what purpose the act was performed for.

sessions.title: An agent is not the principal
sessions.translation: An agent can act in the person’s place within the assigned mandate.
sessions.prompt: What is the careful boundary around agency?
answers: An agent can transmit or perform an assigned act, but the source still defines the mandate and its limits.
An agent can invent new terms for the principal.
Any bystander becomes an agent by observing the transaction.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Representation extends action without erasing the boundaries of authorization.

sessions.title: Historical law needs present-day care
sessions.hebrew: To learn · to understand · not to issue a ruling
sessions.translation: Study to understand; do not treat this lesson as a personal ruling.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy’s responsible stance?
answers: Study document and agency categories historically while directing personal legal concerns to qualified authorities.
Apply an ancient divorce procedure directly to a contemporary case.
Avoid the tractate because its subject is difficult.
sessions.feedback: Serious study can be precise about the past without pretending to replace present-day guidance.

sessions.title: Read an unfamiliar Gittin passage
sessions.translation: Document · agency · intent · delivery · recipient.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for an unfamiliar passage?
answers: Identify the instrument, authorized actor, purpose, delivery act, recipient, and remaining validity question.
Begin with a modern verdict before locating the source’s categories.
Treat writing, agency, and delivery as one undifferentiated act.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Gittin through document identity, agency, intent, validity, and delivery.

halakha.title: Follow a practice through its sources.
halakha.intro: Halakhic learning asks how a broad Torah instruction becomes a structured practice through Mishnah, Gemara, later codes, and ongoing interpretation. This is study support, not personal psak.

sessions.title: Start with a broad command
sessions.hebrew: וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ וּבֵרַכְתָּ אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ
sessions.translation: You shall eat, be satisfied, and bless the Lord your God.
sessions.prompt: What does this verse provide for later halakhic study?
answers: A Torah directive connecting eating, satisfaction, and blessing.
A fixed formula stating which words the blessing must use.
A category system sorting foods by the blessings they take.
sessions.feedback: Good. Begin with what the Torah text says before asking how later sources specify it — the formula and the categories are precisely the later layers’ work.

sessions.title: A Mishnah organizes cases
sessions.translation: How does one recite blessings over fruits?
sessions.prompt: What new work does the Mishnah do?
answers: It organizes a broad practice into categories of cases.
It derives the practice’s obligation from a scriptural verse.
It rules on which opinion to follow when categories conflict.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Mishnah makes practice discussable by sorting kinds of cases — derivation questions belong to Gemara, and decisions between views to the codes.

sessions.title: The category needs explanation
sessions.translation: From where are these matters derived?
sessions.prompt: What does this Gemara question ask for?
answers: A source or reasoning that grounds the practice.
A definition of the categories the Mishnah listed.
A practical sign for when the obligation begins.
sessions.feedback: Right. Mena hanei milei asks for grounding — where does this come from? — not for definitions or practical markers, which other questions pursue.

sessions.title: A code gathers a practice
sessions.translation: It is a positive commandment from the Torah to bless.
sessions.prompt: What role does a legal code typically play?
answers: It states and organizes practice in a later legal form.
It records the debates that produced each practice, voice by voice.
It adds new obligations the earlier sources never discussed.
sessions.feedback: Good. Codes collect and formulate — Rambam famously states conclusions without the arguments, which is exactly why tracing back to the sources matters.

sessions.title: Do not collapse the layers
sessions.translation: Torah · Mishnah · Gemara · code.
sessions.prompt: What is the most useful reason to study the chain?
answers: It shows how practice is interpreted and developed across distinct source genres.
It lets a learner check each layer against the one that came before it.
It reveals which single layer carries the real authority for practice.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Each layer has a different role — the chain is not an error-checking ladder, and no single link replaces the others.

sessions.title: A category meets a new situation
sessions.translation: What is the case?
sessions.prompt: What should a learner do before assuming a source answers a new practical question?
answers: Clarify the facts and identify which source categories and distinctions may matter.
Search the codes for the ruling closest to the situation and adopt it.
Follow the stricter of any two sources that could plausibly apply.
sessions.feedback: Right. Cases matter; practical learning begins with precision about the situation — closest-match and always-stricter are both tempting shortcuts that skip the facts.

sessions.title: Study is not psak
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy’s appropriate role in halakhic study?
answers: Help learners trace sources and reasoning while directing personal practical questions to qualified guidance.
Present every source so learners can reach their own practical rulings.
Teach only theory, leaving all practical topics out of the curriculum.
sessions.feedback: Moral seriousness includes being clear about what learning can do and what it cannot replace — self-ruling and topic-avoidance are opposite ways of erasing the same boundary.

sessions.title: Identify the layer and next question
sessions.hebrew: וּבֵרַכְתָּ · כֵּיצַד מְבָרְכִין · מְנָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי
sessions.translation: You shall bless · how does one bless · from where are these matters derived?
sessions.prompt: What canonical movement do these phrases illustrate?
answers: A Torah directive becomes categorized in Mishnah and then examined for grounding in Gemara.
A Gemara question is answered by a Mishnah, which a verse then confirms.
Three formulations of one rule, restated as each generation received it.
sessions.feedback: You can now see how legal practice becomes a source-based conversation across generations — and the direction of that conversation matters.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: From where are these matters derived?
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this question in a few words.
acceptable: from where are these matters derived
from where are these things derived
where are these matters derived from
from where do we derive this
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

history.kicker: HISTORY ARC · COMMUNITY, MEMORY, AND INSTITUTION
history.title: Place a source in time and community.
history.intro: Jewish History reads a source as evidence about an event, about how it was remembered, and about the communities and institutions that carried it forward — three different questions, not one.

sessions.title: Every source has an audience
sessions.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
sessions.prompt: What historical question should come first with this verse?
answers: Who receives this message, in what political setting, and what response is being asked of them?
What has this verse meant to Jewish communities across later centuries?
Does this verse state a permanent principle or a concession to circumstance?
sessions.feedback: Good. Historical reading starts by locating a source in a human world — reception history and the principle-question are real, but they come after the original audience is found.

sessions.title: A source is not the whole past
sessions.translation: Memory · testimony.
sessions.prompt: What distinction helps a learner read a historical source?
answers: A source may be evidence about an event and also evidence about how someone remembered it.
An eyewitness source outweighs any account recorded generations later.
A source tells you what happened; interpretation begins only afterward.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Sources are both windows and voices — proximity is not automatic reliability, and there is no interpretation-free reading to do first.

sessions.title: Texts travel with people
sessions.translation: Babylonia · Land of Israel.
sessions.prompt: What does this comparison make possible?
answers: Ask how place, language, institutions, and community shape Jewish learning.
Determine which of the two centers preserved the more authentic tradition.
Trace how teachings moved from the older center to the newer one.
sessions.feedback: History helps learners see that texts are studied by communities in particular places — authenticity-ranking and one-way transmission are the tempting oversimplifications.

sessions.title: More than one narrative can exist
sessions.translation: Source · interpretation · evidence.
sessions.prompt: What is a responsible comparison move when two accounts differ?
answers: State what each account claims and what evidence it uses before choosing an interpretation.
Prefer the account whose author stood closest to the events described.
Merge the accounts into one version that preserves details from both.
sessions.feedback: Good. Historical disagreement can be studied through evidence and perspective — proximity-preference and harmonization both skip that work.

sessions.title: Ideas take social form
sessions.translation: Study house · community.
sessions.prompt: What question does this pair invite?
answers: How institutions sustain learning, practice, authority, and belonging across time.
When the study house first appeared, and which community built it.
Whether the study house or the community holds the greater authority.
sessions.feedback: Texts, practices, and institutions shape one another — origins and authority-ranking are narrower questions inside that larger one.

sessions.title: Read it again, with more in view
sessions.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
sessions.prompt: Reading the verse again with institution and memory in view, what new question opens?
answers: How communities institutionalized this instruction over time, and how later communities remembered doing so.
Whether the prophet foresaw the institutions his instruction would create.
Which single institution best fulfilled the verse’s instruction in practice.
sessions.feedback: Right. A source can be reread productively once you have more categories to bring to it — the question is about the communities’ work, not the prophet’s foresight or a ranking.
