sessions.title: A Gemara move, a historical question
sessions.translation: This is in one case; that is in another.
sessions.prompt: This distinction move comes from Gemara study. How might it help compare two historical accounts?
answers: By showing that two accounts that look contradictory may describe genuinely different settings or communities.
By showing that apparent contradictions are usually errors of copying or translation.
By showing that both accounts must be partially true and partially false.
sessions.feedback: A reasoning move built for legal texts can also sharpen historical comparison — the distinction dissolves contradictions by re-mapping cases, not by blaming scribes or splitting differences.

sessions.title: Map the source on your own
sessions.translation: Memory · study house · community.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move across these three fragments?
answers: Ask what event or practice is being remembered, by which community, and through what institution.
Date each fragment, then arrange the three in chronological order.
Identify which of the three terms the other two depend upon.
sessions.feedback: You can now place a source within time, community, memory, and institution on your own — chronology and dependency-hunting are tools, not the map itself.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this instruction in a few words.
acceptable: seek the welfare of the city
seek the peace of the city
and seek the welfare of the city
and seek the peace of the city
seek the wellbeing of the city
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

horayot.kicker: NEZIKIN SOURCE TRAIL · AUTHORITY, ERROR, REPAIR
horayot.title: Read an institutional mistake through authority and responsibility.
horayot.intro: Horayot asks what happens when an authorized court rules in error and a community relies on it. Learn to distinguish jurisdiction, good-faith reliance, responsibility, and correction before drawing modern conclusions.

sessions.title: A court can rule in error
sessions.translation: An erroneous ruling of the court.
sessions.prompt: What should a reader notice first?
answers: The source distinguishes an institutional ruling from an individual mistake.
The text says every disagreement is automatically a court error.
The ruling has no legal consequences because it was unintentional.
sessions.feedback: Right. Horayot begins by asking what happens when an authorized court reaches a mistaken ruling.

sessions.title: Who issued the ruling?
sessions.translation: The high court.
sessions.prompt: Why identify the court before judging the outcome?
answers: Authority and jurisdiction help determine whether reliance and atonement rules apply.
Any speaker has exactly the same institutional status.
Authority is irrelevant once a mistake is discovered.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The tractate makes authority a condition of the legal analysis.

sessions.title: A community follows the ruling
sessions.translation: The people acted on their instruction.
sessions.prompt: What changes when the public acts on the court's instruction?
answers: The source must account for good-faith reliance and communal consequences, not only the court's intent.
Reliance turns every later action into deliberate rebellion.
The court's responsibility disappears because others acted.
sessions.feedback: Good. Horayot tracks how institutional speech travels into communal action.

sessions.title: What kind of error triggers liability?
sessions.translation: What is the reason they erred?
sessions.prompt: What does the Gemara's question invite?
answers: Separate the court's type of error, the issue ruled upon, and the acts that followed.
Assume that every mistake has the same legal result.
Replace the source question with a modern political judgment.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Gemara asks for a precise map of error rather than a blanket label.

sessions.title: Court, public, and individual
sessions.translation: Court · community · individual.
sessions.prompt: Why distinguish these actors?
answers: Different actors may carry different obligations when a mistaken ruling is followed.
The categories are rhetorical and can be collapsed.
Only the individual matters once an outcome occurs.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Responsibility is distributed by role, authority, and reliance.

sessions.title: Correction is part of responsibility
sessions.translation: Return · acknowledgment · repair.
sessions.prompt: What is the best response after discovering a mistaken institutional ruling?
answers: Acknowledge the error, stop extending it, and map the appropriate repair within the source's categories.
Hide the error so institutional authority appears perfect.
Treat correction as proof that all authority is illegitimate.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Responsible authority includes correction, not only initial confidence.

sessions.title: Ancient authority is not a present ruling
sessions.translation: Historical study · not a practical ruling.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy's responsible stance?
answers: Study the tractate's institutional categories historically without presenting them as a current legal decision.
Use an ancient court case to authorize a present action automatically.
Avoid the tractate because institutional error is uncomfortable to examine.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning preserves historical precision and distinguishes study from contemporary authority.

sessions.title: Map an institutional mistake
sessions.translation: Authority · error · reliance · repair.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for an unfamiliar institutional ruling?
answers: Identify authority, jurisdiction, type of error, who relied on it, and what correction follows.
Begin with a verdict about whether institutions are trustworthy.
Treat every mistaken ruling as intentional wrongdoing.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Horayot through authority, reliance, responsibility, and repair.

keritot.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · LIABILITY, KNOWLEDGE, ATONEMENT
keritot.title: Read how knowledge shapes serious liability.
keritot.intro: Keritot follows a counted field of grave transgressions and asks what changes when an act is inadvertent, known, doubtful, or met by a prescribed atonement.

sessions.title: A counted field of liability
sessions.translation: karet · inadvertence · sin-offering
sessions.prompt: What pressure does the opening Mishnah create?
answers: It gathers grave transgressions into a defined category and asks what liability follows when one acts inadvertently.
It says every mistake carries the same penalty regardless of the act.
It treats the list as a narrative with no legal categories.
sessions.feedback: Right. Keritot begins with a counted legal field: serious acts, a defined consequence, and a question about inadvertent performance.

sessions.title: Why thirty-six?
sessions.translation: thirty-six · principal categories
sessions.prompt: What should a reader preserve when the Mishnah counts the transgressions?
answers: The number is a boundary marker: it defines which grave acts belong to this liability system.
The count is only a mnemonic and has no interpretive force.
Every prohibited act automatically belongs in the same count.
sessions.feedback: Good. A counted list is an argument about scope, not merely a memory aid.

sessions.title: Knowing and not knowing
sessions.translation: knowledge · inadvertence · deliberate act
sessions.prompt: Why does the source track what the person knew?
answers: Knowledge and intention distinguish an inadvertent act, which can generate an offering, from a deliberate act with a different path.
Knowledge never changes the legal analysis.
Any act called accidental receives the same consequence even when the person knew the rule.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Keritot makes mental state a legal fact: ignorance, recognition, and deliberate action cannot be collapsed.

sessions.title: Liability is not the offering
sessions.translation: liability · atonement · offering
sessions.prompt: What distinction should remain visible?
answers: First identify the liability; then ask which atonement or offering the Torah assigns to that case.
The offering itself determines whether an act was prohibited.
A person can choose any offering once liability is established.
sessions.feedback: Right. A careful map separates the act, the liability, and the prescribed means of atonement.

sessions.title: Which verse fixes the case?
sessions.translation: what is the reason · from where
sessions.prompt: What does a Gemara source-question invite here?
answers: Ask which scriptural phrase makes the knowledge condition and offering assignment legally decisive.
Replace the verse with a modern intuition about intent.
Ignore the wording because the list is self-explanatory.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Gemara tests the list against its textual basis and asks how the verse controls the case.

sessions.title: One act, more than one condition
sessions.translation: doubt · knowledge · captive child
sessions.prompt: What should a reader test after finding the rule?
answers: Which conditions alter liability or atonement, and which facts leave the original category intact.
Whether one offering must cover every possible knowledge state.
Whether uncertainty can be ignored once an act is named.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Scope work follows the conditions: doubt, later knowledge, and constrained knowledge can change the legal path.

sessions.title: Historical atonement categories
sessions.translation: to learn · to understand · to ask
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of these offering sources?
answers: Study their categories and reasoning as historical textual literacy, not as current ritual instruction.
Treat the ancient offering system as a present-day procedure.
Avoid the legal reasoning because the Temple setting is historical.
sessions.feedback: Serious study honors the precision of the source while distinguishing historical sacrificial law from present practice.

sessions.title: Map liability with care
sessions.translation: act · knowledge · liability · atonement
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new Keritot case?
answers: Name the act, establish knowledge and intention, identify the liability, then test the prescribed atonement and its limits.
Choose an offering first and infer the person’s mental state afterward.
Treat liability, knowledge, and atonement as interchangeable labels.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Keritot by tracking act, mental state, liability, atonement, and boundary in order.

ketubot.kicker: A FIXED DETAIL HIDES AN INSTITUTION
ketubot.title: Read a wedding schedule as a door into legal reasoning.
ketubot.intro: Ketubot opens with a fixed weekday, not a ruling. The Gemara's task — and yours — is to ask what real concern that schedule was built to serve, and to hold more than one real concern at once.

sessions.title: A Mishnah sets a schedule
sessions.hebrew: בְּתוּלָה נִשֵּׂאת לְיוֹם הָרְבִיעִי וְאַלְמָנָה לַחֲמִישִׁי
sessions.translation: A virgin is married on Wednesday, and a widow on Thursday.
sessions.prompt: What kind of information does this opening line provide?
answers: A fixed schedule for two different kinds of marriage, stated before any reason is given.
A list of witnesses required at a wedding.
A biblical quotation about marriage.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Mishnah states a schedule first — the reason behind it is exactly what the Gemara will investigate.

sessions.title: A schedule invites a question
sessions.translation: Why specifically Wednesday?
sessions.prompt: What is the Gemara likely to investigate here?
answers: Why this particular day serves some purpose the Mishnah has not yet explained.
How to spell Wednesday in Hebrew.
Whether the Mishnah has a printing error.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara often turns a fixed, unexplained detail into a question about institutional purpose.

sessions.title: A fixed day, a working court
sessions.hebrew: בָּתֵּי דִינִין יוֹשְׁבִין בָּעֲיָירוֹת בַּשֵּׁנִי וּבַחֲמִישִׁי
sessions.translation: Courts sit in the towns on Monday and Thursday.
sessions.prompt: How does this fact answer the “why Wednesday” question?
answers: A groom with a claim about the marriage could reach a sitting court the very next morning, on Thursday.
It proves the Mishnah is unrelated to courts at all.
It shows that courts never sat on a fixed schedule.
sessions.feedback: Right. Marrying on Wednesday night placed any urgent claim one morning away from a functioning court — the schedule serves a real institutional need.

sessions.title: Court access alone would allow Sunday
sessions.translation: Her honor / dignity.
sessions.prompt: If reaching a sitting court were the only concern, a Sunday wedding would also work, with Monday available for any claim. Why does the Gemara prefer Wednesday over Sunday?
answers: Sunday leaves no ordinary weekday before it for preparing a fitting wedding feast, since it follows Shabbat — so Wednesday balances court access against the bride’s dignity.
The Gemara has no interest in the bride’s experience at all.
Sunday weddings were legally forbidden outright.
sessions.feedback: Good. A single schedule can serve two real values at once — evidentiary access and human dignity — and naming both keeps the reading honest.

sessions.title: Keep the structure visible
sessions.translation: Mishnah · question · reason.
sessions.prompt: Which sequence describes what you just traced across these sources?
answers: A fixed rule, a question about why it exists, then an answer built from real institutional and social concerns.
A final ruling with no discussion at all.
A verse followed by an unrelated story.
sessions.feedback: Good. Naming the sequence — rule, question, reason — is a skill that transfers to nearly every opening sugya in Shas.

sessions.title: Sensitive material needs a clear line
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: Ketubot opens with claims that touch a couple’s private life. What is Jewish Learning Academy’s appropriate role here?
answers: Support careful reading of the sugya’s structure and reasoning while directing any real personal or marital question to qualified guidance.
Use the Mishnah to answer a real question about someone’s marriage.
Avoid the tractate because the subject is sensitive.
sessions.feedback: Right. A tractate can be studied seriously and responsibly without ever standing in for a rabbi, court, or counselor.

sessions.title: A measurement had a reason too
sessions.translation: Because the eye does not take hold of it.
sessions.prompt: You already learned that Eruvin’s twenty-cubit measure has a functional reason. What does that skill let you expect from any fixed detail in a Mishnah?
answers: That a specific number, day, or measure is rarely arbitrary — it is worth asking what real concern it was built to serve.
That every measurement in the Mishnah is decorative.
That reasons behind Mishnaic details are never recoverable.
sessions.feedback: The same habit — treat a fixed detail as a question, not a given — reads Eruvin’s cubits and Ketubot’s weekday with the same discipline.

sessions.title: Map the schedule on your own
sessions.hebrew: בְּתוּלָה נִשֵּׂאת לְיוֹם הָרְבִיעִי · מַאי שְׁנָא · בָּתֵּי דִינִין
sessions.translation: A virgin is married on Wednesday · why different · courts sit.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move across these three fragments?
answers: Name the schedule, ask why it is fixed this way, then look for the institutional or social reason behind it.
Assume the schedule needs no explanation.
Guess the reason before reading the Gemara’s own answer.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a schedule-and-reason sugya with a concrete map.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: Why is it different? / What is different?
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase in a few words.
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

kiddushin.kicker: NASHIM SOURCE TRAIL - ACQUISITION, AGENCY, STATUS
kiddushin.title: Read how a status-changing act is formed.
kiddushin.intro: Kiddushin asks how defined acquisition categories, consent, agency, conditions, and measures work together to establish a status. Learn each category before drawing conclusions.

sessions.title: Acquisition has defined forms
sessions.translation: A woman is acquired through three ways.
sessions.prompt: What does the opening Mishnah ask you to notice?
answers: The source organizes kiddushin through specified acquisition categories rather than an undefined private gesture.
Any gift automatically creates every marriage status.
The categories are only poetic descriptions with no legal work.
sessions.feedback: Right. Kiddushin begins by naming the forms through which a status-changing act is recognized.

sessions.title: An act needs an authorized actor
sessions.translation: A man betroths directly or through his agent.
sessions.prompt: Why does the source distinguish direct action from agency?
answers: It maps who may perform the act and how an authorized agent can stand in for the principal.
Any observer becomes an agent merely by being present.
Agency removes the need for any defined act or recipient.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Agency extends action through a mandate; it does not erase authorization.

sessions.title: A category changes personal status
sessions.translation: You are set apart / betrothed to me.
sessions.prompt: What should a reader track after the formal act?
answers: Which status the source says follows, and which conditions make that status effective.
Whether the phrase sounds emotionally sincere to a modern listener.
Whether every relationship now has the same legal status.
sessions.feedback: Good. The tractate keeps the speech-act and its status consequence connected but distinct.

sessions.title: Objects and measures matter
sessions.translation: With money worth at least a perutah.
sessions.prompt: Why does the source specify a measure?
answers: A defined threshold separates a recognized acquisition act from an insufficient or ambiguous transfer.
Any object has identical force regardless of value.
The measure is optional once the parties agree privately.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Torah categories often work through concrete thresholds that make status legible.

sessions.title: A condition can shape the outcome
sessions.translation: On the condition that…
sessions.prompt: How should a reader approach conditional language?
answers: Identify the condition, when it must be met, and whether the source treats the status as dependent on it.
Assume every condition is merely rhetorical emphasis.
Ignore the condition once the initial words were spoken.
sessions.feedback: Right. Conditional language requires a sequence: act, condition, fulfillment, and status effect.

sessions.title: A representative carries a defined mandate
sessions.translation: A person’s agent is like the person himself.
sessions.prompt: What boundary keeps agency precise?
answers: The agent acts within the principal’s assigned purpose and cannot invent a new status or term.
The agent may change the recipient or condition at will.
Any third party can ratify an act without authorization.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Representation transmits an authorized act; it does not create unlimited power.

sessions.title: Status categories need present-day care
sessions.translation: Study to understand; do not treat this lesson as a practical ruling.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy’s responsible stance?
answers: Study ancient status and agency categories historically while directing personal questions to qualified contemporary authorities.
Apply a source excerpt directly to a present relationship without context.
Avoid the tractate because its status language is difficult.
sessions.feedback: Serious study preserves the text’s categories and acknowledges the limits of an educational lesson.

sessions.title: Read an unfamiliar Kiddushin passage
sessions.translation: Act · agent · condition · status.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for an unfamiliar passage?
answers: Identify the acquisition form, actor and agency, condition, measure, and resulting status before evaluating the dispute.
Begin with a modern conclusion before locating the source categories.
Collapse consent, agency, and status into one undifferentiated idea.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Kiddushin through acquisition categories, agency, conditions, and status effects.

makkot.kicker: NEZIKIN SOURCE TRAIL · TESTIMONY AND CONSEQUENCE
makkot.title: Read a legal category through its source and limit.
makkot.intro: Makkot opens with conspiring witnesses. Follow the Mishnah’s procedure, the Torah phrase that grounds it, the Gemara’s close reading, and the distinction that keeps testimony from being flattened into a slogan.

sessions.title: What makes witnesses zomemim?
sessions.translation: How do witnesses become conspiring witnesses?
sessions.prompt: What kind of question opens the tractate?
answers: A procedural question about how a defined legal status is established.
A general reflection with no category or procedure to follow.
A final judgment that closes the inquiry before a case appears.
sessions.feedback: Right. “How” opens a procedure: expect a category and the conditions that establish it.

sessions.title: The intended consequence returns
sessions.hebrew: וַעֲשִׂיתֶם לוֹ כַּאֲשֶׁר זָמַם לַעֲשׂוֹת לְאָחִיו
sessions.translation: You shall do to him as he schemed to do to his brother.
sessions.prompt: What principle grounds the Mishnaic category?
answers: The intended consequence is applied back to witnesses proven to have schemed it.
A fixed penalty applies without regard to what the witnesses alleged.
Witnesses cannot be accountable once testimony has been given.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Mishnah’s procedure is read through a Torah source with reciprocal logic.

sessions.title: “Schemed,” not “did”
sessions.translation: As he schemed — and not as he did.
sessions.prompt: What boundary does the Gemara draw from this wording?
answers: The verse is read as limiting this consequence to an exposed scheme rather than an accomplished result.
The verse means timing never matters once a witness has spoken.
The Gemara treats the verse as a moral slogan with no legal boundary.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A close reader asks what one word includes, and what it excludes.

sessions.title: Hazama is not simple contradiction
sessions.translation: Exposure by alibi · not mere contradiction.
sessions.prompt: Why does the distinction matter to the source’s logic?
answers: Hazama discredits the witnesses’ presence; a contradiction alone leaves competing accounts.
The terms are interchangeable names for the same refutation.
Any disagreement about facts automatically proves the witnesses schemed.
sessions.feedback: Right. The source distinguishes an attack on the witnesses themselves from a conflict between accounts.

sessions.title: Keep source, category, and limit together
sessions.translation: Testimony · scheme · consequence · boundary.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map of this source?
answers: Name the witness category, trace its Torah source, then state the condition that limits its consequence.
Choose a punishment first and read the source afterward.
Treat every disagreement about testimony as the same case.
sessions.feedback: Good. A serious source map holds category, source, and limit in one view.

sessions.title: Read legal precision responsibly
sessions.translation: Category · source · precision · boundary.
sessions.prompt: Approaching a fresh legal source, which order best protects its reasoning?
answers: Identify the category, locate its source, read the key wording, then test the limit.
Start from a preferred outcome and select phrases that fit it.
Assume one familiar term answers every new case.
sessions.feedback: You can now trace a category through its source and its carefully stated limit.

sessions.title: Return to the source phrase
sessions.translation: As he schemed to do to his brother.
sessions.prompt: Which translation preserves the anchor phrase’s central idea?
answers: As he schemed to do to his brother.
As he did to his brother.
As he thought about his brother.
sessions.feedback: Keep the phrase available: the source’s “schemed” wording carries the category’s reciprocal logic.

megillah.kicker: MOED SOURCE TRAIL · PUBLIC READING AND COMMUNITY
megillah.title: Read a schedule as a map of a community.
megillah.intro: Megillah opens with a reading window rather than one date. Follow the Mishnah’s places and times, then ask why the Gemara makes room for villages to read early.

sessions.title: Five possible days, one bounded window
sessions.hebrew: מגילה נקראת באחד עשר בשנים עשר בשלשה עשר בארבעה עשר ובחמשה עשר
sessions.translation: The Megillah is read on the eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, or fifteenth.
sessions.prompt: What does this opening range tell a careful reader?
answers: The source establishes a bounded reading window whose different dates will need explanation.
The date of reading is completely unstructured.
Five unrelated holidays are being named.
sessions.feedback: Right. A range invites the reader to ask which communities receive which date and why.

sessions.title: Flexibility has an edge
sessions.translation: Not earlier and not later.
sessions.prompt: What job does this phrase perform?
answers: It marks that the range is deliberate and bounded, not an open-ended choice.
It says every community reads on exactly the same day.
It removes the need to explain the range.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Mishnah gives flexibility a defined limit.

sessions.title: Walled cities receive a distinct date
sessions.hebrew: כרכין המוקפין חומה מימות יהושע בן נון קורין בחמשה עשר
sessions.translation: Cities walled from the days of Joshua son of Nun read on the fifteenth.
sessions.prompt: What should you map before trying to explain this rule?
answers: The community category, its historical anchor, and the date attached to it.
Only the number fifteen.
A modern ruling for every walled city.
sessions.feedback: Good. Keep category, anchor, and assigned date together.

sessions.title: Villages move to an assembly day
sessions.translation: Rather, the villages advance to the day of assembly.
sessions.prompt: What kind of move is this?
answers: A stated accommodation for one community within the Mishnah’s overall schedule.
A rejection of all dates in the Mishnah.
A personal suggestion without communal context.
sessions.feedback: Right. The exception is structured: a named community, a particular kind of day, and a place in the larger schedule.

sessions.title: Gemara asks about the early date
sessions.translation: The Megillah is read on the eleventh—where do we derive this?
sessions.prompt: What is the Gemara asking for?
answers: Why the early eleventh-day reading belongs within the Mishnah’s stated window.
Whether the Megillah exists.
A way to ignore the Mishnah’s schedule.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara targets the exceptional early reading, not the entire Mishnah.

sessions.title: Flexibility is connected to shared provision
sessions.hebrew: כדי שיספקו מים ומזון לאחיהם שבכרכין
sessions.translation: So that they could supply water and food to their brothers in the cities.
sessions.prompt: What does this reason show about the earlier reading?
answers: The accommodation is tied to a practical relationship between villages and cities.
The early date makes the observance less important.
The schedule has no connection to communal life.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Gemara explains the date through an ordinary communal function.

sessions.title: Map a flexible public rule
sessions.translation: Time · place · community · need.
sessions.prompt: How should you first read a new source with a main rule and a special schedule for one group?
answers: Name the default schedule, identify the community exception, and ask what need or function explains it.
Assume the exception erases the main rule.
Treat the source as individual advice.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a public schedule as a map of categories, accommodations, and stated reasons.

sessions.title: Recall the Gemara’s focus
sessions.translation: From where do we derive this?
sessions.prompt: What does this question ask a learner to seek?
answers: The basis or explanation for a specific feature the source has just stated.
The easiest date to choose today.
A reason to stop mapping the Mishnah.
sessions.feedback: Good. The question directs attention back to the source feature that needs grounding.

meilah.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · MISUSE, AWARENESS, RESTITUTION
meilah.title: Read the breach of consecrated property.
meilah.intro: Meilah follows what happens when someone benefits from sacred property. Track sanctity, awareness, restitution, and the conditions that define misuse.

sessions.title: Using what is not yours
sessions.translation: misuse · consecrated property · inadvertence
sessions.prompt: What pressure does the opening case create?
answers: It asks what happens when someone derives benefit from property whose sacred status still governs it.
It says sacred property becomes ordinary once someone touches it.
It treats every use as intentional theft.
sessions.feedback: Right. Meilah begins with benefit from consecrated property and asks what legal breach follows.

sessions.title: Disqualification does not erase holiness
sessions.translation: sacred · disqualified · sanctity
sessions.prompt: What should a reader keep distinct?
answers: A disqualified offering can remain sacred; validity and sanctity are separate legal questions.
Once an offering is disqualified, every sacred status disappears.
Sanctity is only a description of ritual quality.
sessions.feedback: Good. Meilah requires the reader to preserve sanctity even when an offering is no longer valid for its original use.

sessions.title: Accident and intention
sessions.translation: inadvertence · deliberate act · knowledge
sessions.prompt: Why does the source track what the person knew?
answers: Awareness separates inadvertent misuse, with its prescribed liability, from deliberate misuse with a different legal path.
Knowledge never changes the consequence of using sacred property.
Calling an act accidental makes the mental state irrelevant.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Meilah makes knowledge a legal fact: inadvertence and deliberate misuse cannot be collapsed.

sessions.title: Benefit is not ownership
sessions.translation: benefit · possession · consecrated property
sessions.prompt: What distinction should remain visible?
answers: Receiving benefit can trigger meilah even though the property never becomes ordinary private ownership.
Any benefit automatically transfers ownership from the sacred treasury.
Only physical theft can count as misuse.
sessions.feedback: Right. The legal issue is unauthorized benefit, not a simple transfer of ownership.

sessions.title: Why does restitution follow?
sessions.translation: what is the reason · guilt-offering · fifth
sessions.prompt: What does a Gemara source-question invite here?
answers: Ask which verse makes restitution and the added fifth responsive to the sacred breach.
Replace the verse with a general rule about property damage.
Ignore the wording because restitution is only a practical custom.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Gemara presses for the textual basis of returning value and adding the prescribed fifth.

sessions.title: What counts as benefit?
sessions.hebrew: shiur · hanaah · davar sheyesh bo mamash
sessions.translation: measure · benefit · tangible object
sessions.prompt: What should a reader test after finding the rule?
answers: Which measurable benefit and conditions make the misuse liable, and which cases remain outside the rule.
Whether every contact with sacred property creates identical liability.
Whether the value or context of the benefit can be ignored.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Scope work asks what benefit occurred, whether it reaches the measure, and which conditions qualify the rule.

sessions.title: Historical sacred-property categories
sessions.translation: to learn · to understand · to ask
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of these sources?
answers: Study their categories and reasoning as historical textual literacy, not as current Temple-treasury procedure.
Treat the ancient restitution system as a present-day ritual instruction.
Avoid the legal reasoning because the Temple setting is historical.
sessions.feedback: Serious study honors the precision of the source while distinguishing historical Temple law from present practice.

sessions.title: Map misuse with care
sessions.translation: act · knowledge · benefit · restitution
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new Meilah case?
answers: Name the sacred property, identify the benefit and awareness, then determine liability, restitution, and the boundary.
Choose restitution first and infer whether benefit occurred afterward.
Treat inadvertent and intentional misuse as interchangeable.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Meilah by tracking status, benefit, awareness, restitution, and boundary in order.

menachot.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · PARALLEL, EXCEPTION, TRANSFER
menachot.title: Carry a legal structure forward—then let the new source correct it.
menachot.intro: Menachot opens with a parallel case of designated purpose in meal-offerings. Transfer Zevachim’s distinction carefully, identify the exceptions, and learn why a parallel never excuses close reading.

sessions.title: The same pressure in meal-offerings
sessions.translation: All meal-offerings from which a handful was taken not for their proper purpose.
sessions.prompt: What does Menachot’s opening invite a learner who has studied Zevachim to notice?
answers: A familiar question about an act performed for a mismatched designated purpose.
A source with no relation to the earlier intention distinction.
A rule that makes purpose irrelevant in every offering.
sessions.feedback: Right. The source gives a new offering type while preserving a recognizable legal pressure.

sessions.title: Valid, yet not counted
sessions.hebrew: כְּשֵׁרוֹת אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא עָלוּ לַבְּעָלִים לְשֵׁם חוֹבָה
sessions.translation: Valid, but they did not count for the owners toward their obligation.
sessions.prompt: Which distinction transfers directly from Zevachim into this line?
answers: The act may remain valid while still failing to fulfill the owner’s obligation.
Any valid act automatically fulfills every obligation.
The source has removed the question of legal outcome.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Transfer begins by recognizing a structure that the new text actually repeats.

sessions.title: A parallel is not identity
sessions.translation: Valid · obligation.
sessions.prompt: What must a careful reader avoid after seeing a strong parallel?
answers: Assuming that every later rule and exception in the two tractates will be identical.
Using the earlier distinction to orient the new case.
Reading Menachot’s own words for their specific limits.
sessions.feedback: Good. A parallel gives a starting map, not permission to stop reading.

sessions.title: Two offerings break the broad rule
sessions.translation: Except for the sinner’s meal-offering and the jealousy offering.
sessions.prompt: What does the Mishnah require when it says “except”?
answers: Revise the broad map by marking cases whose result differs from the general pattern.
Discard the whole parallel as useless.
Treat the exception as decorative language with no legal work.
sessions.feedback: Right. Exceptions make the scope of a rule visible.

sessions.title: Purpose can become constitutive
sessions.translation: A sinner’s meal-offering · the jealousy offering.
sessions.prompt: What question should guide the reader when these named offerings receive a different result?
answers: What role does the designated purpose play in defining these particular offerings?
Which offering has the more memorable title?
How to erase the broad rule before examining the cases.
sessions.feedback: Good. The exception directs attention to the relation between an offering’s identity and its purpose.

sessions.title: The parallel needs a reason
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: After locating a broad rule and its exceptions, what does a Gemara reason-question ask you to investigate?
answers: What principle explains both the shared structure and the cases where it changes.
Which outcome is easier to remember without examining the text.
Whether the Mishnah’s distinctions can now be ignored.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A reason-question tests why the rule has this scope rather than another one.

sessions.title: Historical categories, serious study
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible way to use this Temple-service source?
answers: Study its categories and reasoning as historical textual literacy.
Treat it as instructions for contemporary ritual performance.
Avoid its reasoning because its historical setting makes it unlearnable.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning preserves both the source’s reasoning and the boundary of its setting.

sessions.title: Use structure, verify content
sessions.translation: Structure · exception · verification.
sessions.prompt: You meet a new source that strongly resembles one you already know. What is the best first move?
answers: Transfer the shared structure, then identify and test the new source’s own exceptions.
Copy the prior source’s conclusions over without reading the new text closely.
Ignore the resemblance and rebuild every distinction from nothing.
sessions.feedback: You can now use a parallel as a disciplined reading tool: carry the structure forward, then verify the local content.

moed-katan.pageTitle: Jewish Learning Academy · Moed Katan Arc
moed-katan.kicker: MOED SOURCE TRAIL · DEFAULT, LOSS, LIMIT
moed-katan.title: Read a permitted exception without losing the rule it qualifies.
moed-katan.intro: Moed Katan opens with work during Chol HaMoed. Follow the default restraint, the threatened loss, and the limit that keeps an exception from swallowing the festival.

sessions.title: Watering during Chol HaMoed
sessions.translation: One may water an irrigated field during the intermediate festival days.
sessions.prompt: What makes this opening permission worth noticing?
answers: It names work allowed during days when ordinary labor is limited.
It says every kind of agricultural work is identical.
It treats the festival as unrelated to ordinary life.
sessions.feedback: Right. An explicit permission matters because it appears within a setting of restraint.

sessions.title: Permission points back to restraint
sessions.translation: Festival · permission.
sessions.prompt: Before explaining the exception, what should a reader keep in view?
answers: The default restraint that makes this permission a real exception.
Only the permitted act and none of its setting.
A claim that all work is prohibited in every circumstance.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. An exception can only be read clearly against the rule it qualifies.

sessions.title: A matter that would be lost
sessions.translation: A matter that would be lost.
sessions.prompt: What question does the category of threatened loss make the reader ask?
answers: What concrete harm delay would cause in this particular case.
Which activity feels most productive to a worker.
Whether the festival has any limits at all.
sessions.feedback: Good. The category directs attention to the loss the delay is meant to prevent.

sessions.title: Not every convenience is loss
sessions.translation: Loss · convenience.
sessions.prompt: Which distinction keeps the loss category from becoming a blanket permission?
answers: A real threatened loss is different from ordinary convenience or preference.
Any work someone prefers is automatically a threatened loss.
The source is only concerned with symbolic ritual actions.
sessions.feedback: Yes. The category narrows the permission to a specific pressure, not every useful task.

sessions.title: The Mishnah names what it excludes
sessions.translation: Not from rainwater.
sessions.prompt: What is the reader’s first job when the Mishnah adds a limit to a permission?
answers: Ask how the added detail protects the shape of the exception.
Treat the detail as proof that the permission was never real.
Ignore it because the opening permission is more memorable.
sessions.feedback: Right. Limits reveal how an exception is being controlled rather than casually expanded.

sessions.title: A permitted end can still have a limit
sessions.translation: Exertion · festival.
sessions.prompt: Why might a source permit one way of preventing loss but limit a more burdensome one?
answers: The exception must still preserve the festival’s character and restraint.
Any more difficult method is automatically more legally correct.
The distinction proves that preventing loss never matters.
sessions.feedback: Good. A qualified permission can protect against loss without turning the occasion into ordinary labor.

sessions.title: Study is not a personal ruling
sessions.ref: Jewish Learning Academy Moed Katan boundary
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of this tractate’s categories?
answers: Study the source and seek qualified guidance for practical observance.
Apply this lesson directly to a personal work decision.
Assume historical categories have no moral or legal weight.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning includes recognizing when a textual category is not personal guidance.

sessions.title: Map a new exception
sessions.hebrew: כְּלָל · יוֹצֵא מִן הַכְּלָל · טַעַם · גְּבוּל
sessions.translation: Rule · exception · reason · limit.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new source that permits an act within a general restraint?
answers: State the default, identify the pressure, then test the permission’s limit.
Start with the exception and assume the default no longer matters.
Choose the easiest practical result before reading the source.
sessions.feedback: You can now follow how a source makes room for an exception without erasing the rule.

mussar.kicker: MUSSAR ARC · HUMILITY, COURAGE, AND HABIT
mussar.title: Trace a middah from source to habit.
mussar.intro: Mussar study moves from naming a trait, to noticing the tension inside it, to a real situation, to repeated practice, and finally to honest reflection that does not collapse into self-judgment.

sessions.title: Humility is a reading question
sessions.translation: Walk humbly with your God.
sessions.prompt: What does a Mussar learner ask first about a middah like this one?
answers: What kind of humility does this source describe, and what does it exclude?
How can I practice humility in my daily routines starting today?
Which biblical figures best exemplify the humility this verse commands?
sessions.feedback: Good. A middah must be defined before it can form a person — jumping to practice or to exemplars before definition builds the wrong trait carefully.

sessions.title: Humility is not passivity
sessions.translation: The shy person does not learn.
sessions.prompt: What tension does this source create with the humility just named?
answers: Humility can coexist with the courage to ask and participate.
Learning requires setting humility aside inside the study hall.
Shyness is simply a milder, safer form of the same humility.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Ethical traits need nuance — the tempting mistakes are to oppose humility to learning, or to mistake shyness for humility. The source blocks both.

sessions.title: A trait meets a moment
sessions.translation: Human dignity.
sessions.prompt: What should a learner ask before applying humility to a real situation?
answers: Which facts matter, what values are in tension, and what the source actually claims.
Which response the most humble person imaginable would choose here.
Whether the situation is significant enough to warrant a middah at all.
sessions.feedback: Mussar becomes serious when sources meet real complexity — maximal-humility reasoning skips the competing values, and no situation is beneath character.

sessions.title: Small repetition matters
sessions.translation: One mitzvah leads to another mitzvah.
sessions.prompt: How does this source connect humility to ongoing practice?
answers: Repeated small acts of humility can shape attention and future choices.
A significant act of humility outweighs many small routine ones.
Habits sustain a trait only after the trait has fully formed.
sessions.feedback: Good. Mussar asks how repeated practice forms a person over time — the source’s claim is that acts generate acts, not that magnitude or completion comes first.

sessions.title: Evidence is not self-worth
sessions.translation: Accountability · kindness.
sessions.prompt: What is a healthy reflective move after noticing a lapse in humility?
answers: Notice the pattern honestly and return to a source without turning reflection into self-condemnation.
Resolve to try harder, and keep the lapse in mind as motivation.
Balance the lapse against recent successes to keep an accurate score.
sessions.feedback: Moral growth needs both accountability and compassion — willpower resolutions and scorekeeping are the two most tempting substitutes for actually returning to the source.

sessions.title: Humility does not stand alone
sessions.translation: Do justice and love kindness.
sessions.prompt: How does this fuller verse extend the humility source from step one?
answers: It places humility alongside justice and kindness as three linked demands, not one isolated trait.
It ranks the three demands, with justice first and humility last.
It shows humility to be the source from which the other two flow.
sessions.feedback: Right. A middah is rarely isolated — and the verse links the three without ranking them or deriving two from one, though both readings tempt.

sessions.title: A Chassidic source, a Mussar question
sessions.translation: Be as careful with a light commandment as with a weighty one.
sessions.prompt: This source is also read in Chassidus. What Mussar-style question does it raise here?
answers: Whether small, easily dismissed acts of humility deserve the same seriousness as visibly important ones.
Whether the distinction between light and weighty commandments should be abandoned.
Whether care in practice matters more than the inner state behind the practice.
sessions.feedback: The same source can open different, equally serious questions in different subjects — this one extends care to small acts without erasing the light/weighty distinction itself.

sessions.title: Map the trait on your own
sessions.hebrew: וְהַצְנֵעַ לֶכֶת · לֹא הַבַּיְשָׁן לָמֵד · כָּבוֹד הַבְּרִיּוֹת
sessions.translation: Walk humbly · the shy person does not learn · human dignity.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move across these three fragments?
answers: Name the trait, notice the tension it creates, and ask what situation would test it.
Find the shared word that links the three fragments into one teaching.
Order the fragments from the earliest source to the latest one.
sessions.feedback: You can now trace a middah from source, to tension, to a real situation, on your own — word-hunting and chronology are real tools, but not the middah map.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: Walk humbly with your God.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase in a few words.
acceptable: to walk humbly with your god
and walk humbly with your god
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

nazir.kicker: NASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · STATUS, WORDING, TRANSFER
nazir.title: Transfer a reading skill into a new legal status.
nazir.intro: Nazir begins with the same substitute-language structure as Nedarim. Follow what carries over, what changes when speech creates a new status, and where source study must stop short of personal practice.

sessions.title: A familiar rule, a new status
sessions.translation: All substitute terms for nazirite vows are like nazirite vows.
sessions.prompt: What does the Mishnah establish about substitute terms here?
answers: A substitute term can create nazirite status when used as the source recognizes it.
Only the exact word nazir can ever have legal meaning.
Nazirite status cannot be accepted through speech.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Mishnah again treats a legally understood substitute expression as significant.

sessions.title: Nedarim taught this structure
sessions.translation: Substitute vow terms · substitute nazirite terms.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible transfer from Nedarim to Nazir?
answers: The reader can reuse the function-of-language question in a new legal setting.
The two tractates therefore describe one identical legal status.
A familiar opening means the remaining details no longer matter.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Transfer carries a reading move forward while still noticing what the new tractate changes.

sessions.title: Speech can create a status
sessions.translation: Nazirite status.
sessions.prompt: Why distinguish the utterance from the status it creates?
answers: The wording is an entry point, while the status has source-defined consequences.
A status is simply another name for any spoken word.
Once a status is named, the wording no longer needs reading.
sessions.feedback: Good. The source asks the reader to follow both the speech act and the category it brings into view.

sessions.title: An unspecified duration
sessions.translation: An unspecified nazirite vow is thirty days.
sessions.prompt: What kind of reasoning move is a default duration?
answers: It supplies a measure when the source recognizes an unspecified status.
It proves an unspecified declaration has no possible meaning.
It lets each reader invent a duration after the fact.
sessions.feedback: Right. A default gives structured content to an incomplete specification.

sessions.title: Shared language does not erase difference
sessions.translation: Similarity · difference.
sessions.prompt: What should a learner do after recognizing the same opening structure in two tractates?
answers: Ask which later details preserve the pattern and which define the status differently.
Assume all later rules must now be interchangeable.
Stop reading once the shared words are recognized.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Good comparison preserves both shared structure and tractate-specific consequences.

sessions.title: Why sequence matters
sessions.translation: Utterance · measure · consequence.
sessions.prompt: Why follow an effective utterance into its measure and consequences?
answers: Later details show what kind of status the opening words actually create.
The details make the opening rule unnecessary.
Consequences are unrelated to a named category.
sessions.feedback: Good. The sequence keeps a learner from mistaking a language rule for the whole discussion.

sessions.title: Study is not a personal vow
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of this tractate’s source material?
answers: Study its categories and seek qualified guidance for any real question about vows.
Use this lesson alone to decide whether to take on a nazirite status.
Avoid the tractate because live categories cannot be studied responsibly.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning includes knowing that an ancient legal source is not personal guidance.

sessions.title: Map a neighboring source
sessions.translation: Utterance · status · measure · limit.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a source where an utterance may create legal status?
answers: Identify the utterance, name the status, trace its measure, then test the limit.
Treat every familiar term as enough to decide the case.
Begin by applying the source to a personal situation.
sessions.feedback: You can now carry a reading skill across tractates without flattening different legal worlds.

nedarim.kicker: NASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · WORD, INTENT, CATEGORY
nedarim.title: Read legal speech by the work its words perform.
nedarim.intro: Nedarim opens with substitute terms for vows. Learn to distinguish a word’s surface form, its understood function, competing explanations of that function, and the boundary of live practice.

sessions.title: Substitute words can work
sessions.translation: All substitute terms for vows are like vows.
sessions.prompt: What does the Mishnah establish about substitute vow-language?
answers: A substitute term can carry the legal function of a vow.
Only one fixed formula can have any legal effect.
A substitute term automatically cancels every vow.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Mishnah begins by treating function, not one preferred sound, as legally significant.

sessions.title: More than a familiar word
sessions.translation: Substitute term · vow.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first question when a source recognizes substitute language?
answers: What legal work the utterance is understood to perform.
Which version of the word is easiest to pronounce.
Whether all spoken language is legally identical.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The reader asks what a phrase does in context before judging it by surface form alone.

sessions.title: Words operate in a setting
sessions.translation: Utterance · intention.
sessions.prompt: Why is the source’s context important when studying effective speech?
answers: The same sounds can be understood differently depending on how they function in context.
Context never matters once a word has been spoken.
Only a speaker’s private feeling matters, never the utterance.
sessions.feedback: Good. Legal speech is read as an act in context, not as a word list detached from use.

sessions.title: Where do the substitute terms come from?
sessions.translation: Languages of the nations · an enactment of the sages.
sessions.prompt: What do competing accounts of substitute terms ask the learner to distinguish?
answers: Whether their force comes from common usage or deliberate rabbinic enactment.
Whether either account permits learners to make personal vows.
Which explanation uses the oldest Hebrew letters.
sessions.feedback: Right. The disagreement concerns the source of legal force, not merely a vocabulary detail.

sessions.title: Origins shape the next question
sessions.translation: Source · consequence.
sessions.prompt: Why does a Gemara reader keep both accounts visible before deciding a later case?
answers: Each account may explain differently why a new expression is included or excluded.
A disagreement about origins never affects later reasoning.
One account must be ignored as soon as another is mentioned.
sessions.feedback: Yes. A reason matters because it can change the range of cases the category reaches.

sessions.title: A category is not a shortcut
sessions.translation: Discussion · boundary.
sessions.prompt: What protects a reader from turning “substitute term” into an unlimited rule?
answers: Testing the source’s stated category against the details and limits of the case.
Assuming every informal phrase must have the same force.
Using a memorable label instead of reading the source.
sessions.feedback: Good. Categories organize cases, but their scope must be read from the source’s reasoning.

sessions.title: Study is not a personal ruling
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of this tractate’s discussion of vows?
answers: Study the source and seek qualified guidance for real vows or releases.
Use the lesson to decide whether a personal statement is binding.
Avoid the source because its subject has practical consequences.
sessions.feedback: Serious textual study includes not treating a source lesson as personal halakhic advice.

sessions.title: Read a new speech category
sessions.translation: Word · context · function · limit.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a source about legally meaningful speech?
answers: State the utterance, read its context, identify its function, then test its limit.
Choose the most familiar word before reading the source.
Assume all related language has the same legal result.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a speech category without reducing it to either a magic word or a private feeling.

niddah.title: Read a three-way dispute without flattening it.
niddah.intro: Niddah opens mid-argument: Shammai, Beit Hillel, and the Sages each measure a period of uncertainty from a different point. Holding all three positions accurately, without collapsing them into one, is the reading skill this arc builds.

sessions.title: A tractate can open with a dispute
sessions.translation: Shammai says: her time suffices.
sessions.prompt: What does it mean that Niddah opens with a named position rather than an agreed rule?
answers: The tractate begins in the middle of a live disagreement about how far back a period of uncertainty should reach.
The Mishnah is quoting Shammai only to reject him without discussion.
There is no real disagreement; this is simply the accepted rule.
sessions.feedback: Right. Opening with “Shammai says” signals a dispute the Mishnah expects you to track, not a settled ruling.

sessions.title: Hillel answers differently
sessions.translation: And Beit Hillel say: from examination to examination.
sessions.prompt: How does Hillel’s position differ in structure from Shammai’s?
answers: Shammai measures uncertainty from the moment of discovery forward; Hillel measures it backward to the last time she checked, however long ago that was.
Hillel agrees completely with Shammai but uses different words.
Hillel’s position removes the concept of uncertainty entirely.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Two real positions, calculating the same uncertainty from two different reference points — a genuine, recorded machloket.

sessions.title: A third position, not just a vote
sessions.hebrew: וַחֲכָמִים אוֹמְרִים … מֵעֵת לְעֵת מְמַעֵט עַל יַד מִפְּקִידָה לִפְקִידָה
sessions.translation: And the Sages say: a twenty-four hour span reduces the count compared to from-examination-to-examination.
sessions.prompt: What kind of position do the Sages take here?
answers: A structured middle position that uses whichever of the two measures is shorter, rather than simply picking one side.
An exact repetition of Beit Hillel’s position.
A rejection of the entire question as unanswerable.
sessions.feedback: Good. A third Tannaitic voice is not always a compromise vote — here it constructs its own rule from parts of both earlier positions.

sessions.title: Three real positions, not one blurred answer
sessions.translation: Shammai · Hillel · the Sages.
sessions.prompt: What does a disciplined reading of this three-way dispute require?
answers: Naming what each position actually measures, without assuming one obviously wins or that all three are secretly saying the same thing.
Picking whichever position sounds simplest and ignoring the other two.
Concluding that Tannaitic disputes are never worth tracking in detail.
sessions.feedback: This is what careful machloket-reading looks like: three distinct measuring points, each preserved on its own terms.

sessions.title: A presumption from later in the tractate
sessions.translation: All women are presumed to be in a state of purity for their husbands.
sessions.prompt: This is a different Mishnah from the opening dispute. What should a careful reader do before connecting the two?
answers: Check the actual citation and confirm what this presumption applies to before assuming it settles the earlier dispute.
Assume both lines are the same Mishnah since they discuss the same tractate.
Ignore the citation, since exact chapter and verse never matter.
sessions.feedback: Good instinct. This principle comes from Mishnah Niddah 2:4, not the opening Mishnah — precise citation is part of responsible source work.

sessions.title: A presumption still needs a measuring rule
sessions.translation: Her time suffices · presumed pure.
sessions.prompt: How do the opening dispute and this later presumption relate?
answers: The presumption tells you the default status; the opening dispute tells you how far back to recalculate that status once uncertainty arises.
The presumption makes the entire opening dispute irrelevant.
They contradict each other and cannot both be true.
sessions.feedback: Right. A general presumption and a specific measuring rule can operate together without collapsing into a single idea.

sessions.title: Sensitive material needs a clear line
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: Niddah addresses deeply personal and halakhically consequential material. What is Jewish Learning Academy’s appropriate role?
answers: Support careful reading of the sugya’s structure and reasoning while directing any real personal question to a qualified rabbinic authority.
Use the Mishnah’s positions to answer a real personal question directly.
Avoid the tractate entirely because the subject is sensitive.
sessions.feedback: Right. A tractate this consequential can be studied seriously and responsibly without ever standing in for qualified guidance.

sessions.title: You have held a real machloket before
sessions.translation: A great principle · in the likeness of God.
sessions.prompt: You already learned to hold Rabbi Akiva’s and Ben Azzai’s positions without flattening one into the other. What does that habit add here?
answers: A recorded machloket with named positions is not a problem to resolve quickly — it rewards tracking exactly what each side measures or claims.
Machlokot always have one obviously correct side that the other named sages simply missed.
Once one machloket is understood, all others in Shas work identically.
sessions.feedback: The same discipline — preserve each position’s real claim — reads a values-dispute in Chassidus and a measuring-rule dispute in Niddah alike.

sessions.title: Map the dispute on your own
sessions.hebrew: דַּיָּהּ שְׁעָתָהּ · מִפְּקִידָה לִפְקִידָה · מֵעֵת לְעֵת
sessions.translation: Her time suffices · from examination to examination · a twenty-four hour span.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move across these three fragments?
answers: Name each position, identify exactly what point in time each one measures from, then compare them without merging them.
Pick whichever fragment is shortest and treat it as the ruling.
Assume all three fragments say the same thing in different words.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a three-way measuring-rule dispute with a concrete map.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: From examination to examination.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase in a few words.
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

pesachim.kicker: GATEWAY TRACTATE · TIME AND RITUAL ACTION
pesachim.title: Read a legal world built from timing.
pesachim.intro: Pesachim teaches a Gemara-reading skill distinct from Shabbat and Eruvin: separating an action from its time and its tool, and testing a short, ambiguous word against its context.

sessions.title: Begin with the required action
sessions.hebrew: אור לארבעה עשר בודקין את החמץ לאור הנר
sessions.translation: On the eve of the fourteenth, one searches for leaven by the light of a lamp.
sessions.prompt: What does the Mishnah tell a person to do, before any of the details are analyzed?
answers: Search for chametz.
Eat the Passover offering.
Recite the evening Shema.
sessions.feedback: Correct. First identify the required action before analyzing its timing or details.

sessions.title: One short word, more than one meaning
sessions.translation: Light / the eve.
sessions.prompt: Why might a single short word like this need extra attention?
answers: It carries more than one shade of meaning, and the surrounding case has to clarify which one is meant.
It never appears anywhere else in the Mishnah.
It has exactly one possible meaning in every context.
sessions.feedback: Right. Short words often do the most ambiguous work — that is exactly why Gemara slows down over them.

sessions.title: Two supporting details, two jobs
sessions.translation: On the eve of the fourteenth · by the light of a lamp.
sessions.prompt: What two supporting details does a learner need to separate here?
answers: The time of the action and the tool used to perform it.
Two unrelated actions performed by two different people.
A ruling and the reason for the ruling.
sessions.feedback: Yes. This is a core close-reading habit: separate action, time, and instrument.

sessions.title: A word invites a responsible question
sessions.translation: Light / the eve.
sessions.prompt: What is a responsible next question about a short word like this?
answers: What does this word mean here, and how does the surrounding Mishnah clarify it?
Which later law should we decide without reading the discussion?
Can we ignore the word because the action is clear?
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Gemara often slows down over a compact word and tests it against the context and sources.

sessions.title: A clear instruction can still need a reason
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: Why does the Gemara ask for a reason even when the Mishnah’s instruction already seems clear?
answers: The reason determines whether the same rule extends to a case the Mishnah did not explicitly state.
Reasons are only asked for when the Mishnah is confusing.
The question means the Mishnah is incorrect.
sessions.feedback: Right. A stated reason lets a rule travel responsibly to a case the Mishnah never mentioned.

sessions.title: A baraita can sharpen a practice
sessions.translation: It was taught.
sessions.prompt: If a baraita entered the discussion here, what would its most likely job be?
answers: To add, clarify, or challenge the Mishnah’s timing or method.
To cancel the Mishnah entirely.
To introduce an unrelated festival.
sessions.feedback: Good. A cited teaching has a job in the current discussion, not a life of its own.

sessions.title: How far does the search obligation reach?
sessions.hebrew: אֵין חוֹשְׁשִׁין שֶׁמָּא גָּרְרָה חֻלְדָּה מִבַּיִת לְבַיִת
sessions.translation: We are not concerned that perhaps a weasel dragged [chametz] from house to house.
sessions.prompt: After establishing the search itself, what new question does the Mishnah raise?
answers: How far a person’s responsibility for a thorough search actually extends.
Whether searching for chametz is required at all.
What time of day the search must begin.
sessions.feedback: Right. Once an obligation is established, the next real question is always its limit.

sessions.title: A limit needs its own logic
sessions.translation: There is no end to the matter.
sessions.prompt: What legal reasoning move does this phrase name?
answers: A limiting principle: if a concern were followed to its logical extreme, no practical rule could ever be satisfied, so a reasonable boundary is set instead.
A statement that the search for chametz never actually ends.
A rule with no connection to the weasel case at all.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. “There is no end to the matter” is a recurring Talmudic move for drawing a reasonable line around an open-ended worry.

sessions.title: Domain vocabulary, a new setting
sessions.translation: Inside · outside.
sessions.prompt: This distinction comes from Shabbat, not Pesachim. What shared skill does reading it require?
answers: Separate the concrete facts of a case from the ruling before deciding what changes the outcome.
Assume every tractate uses this exact pair of words.
Ignore location since Pesachim is about time, not space.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Time, tool, and place are all variables the same close-reading habit can track.

sessions.title: Map the case on your own
sessions.hebrew: אור לארבעה עשר · לאור הנר · בודקין
sessions.translation: On the eve of the fourteenth · by the light of a lamp · one searches.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move with this case?
answers: Separate the action, its time, and the tool used to perform it before asking why.
Guess the ruling from the first word alone.
Assume the case has already been fully explained.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a time-and-action sugya with a concrete map.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: Light / the eve.
sessions.prompt: Which meaning fits this opening word in the source?
answers: Light / the eve.
A courtyard boundary.
A final legal ruling.
sessions.feedback: You can recognize the word’s meaning from the source, rather than merely guess from a familiar topic.

rosh-hashanah.pageTitle: Jewish Learning Academy · Rosh Hashanah Arc
rosh-hashanah.kicker: MOED SOURCE TRAIL · CALENDAR AND PUBLIC RECORD
rosh-hashanah.title: Read a calendar as a legal map.
rosh-hashanah.intro: Rosh Hashanah starts with a surprising claim: one “new year” can serve several distinct fields. Follow the Mishnah’s categories, then see the Gemara ask what a date actually does in a public record.

sessions.title: Four new years, each with a job
sessions.translation: There are four new years.
sessions.prompt: What does the Mishnah’s opening count ask a reader to expect?
answers: Several distinct calendar functions, not one universal meaning of “new year.”
Four competing names for one identical date.
A story that has no categories to map.
sessions.feedback: Right. A count at the opening often announces a field the Mishnah will sort into categories.

sessions.title: A date is attached to a domain
sessions.hebrew: באחד בניסן ראש השנה למלכים ולרגלים
sessions.translation: On the first of Nisan is the new year for kings and for festivals.
sessions.prompt: What is the first reading move with this date?
answers: Attach the date to the domains it organizes before treating it as a general celebration date.
Assume Nisan is the only new year that matters in the Mishnah.
Ignore the phrase after the date because dates explain themselves.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The date becomes meaningful through the field it orders.

sessions.title: Animal tithe has its own year
sessions.hebrew: באחד באלול ראש השנה למעשר בהמה
sessions.translation: On the first of Elul is the new year for animal tithe.
sessions.prompt: Why is this line not simply another example of the Nisan rule?
answers: It names a different domain with its own counting boundary.
It proves all calendar dates have the same legal use.
It replaces the Mishnah’s opening count.
sessions.feedback: Good. Preserve the domain before comparing the dates.

sessions.title: One date can organize several kinds of counting
sessions.hebrew: באחד בתשרי ראש השנה לשנים ולשמיטין וליובלות
sessions.translation: On the first of Tishrei is the new year for years, sabbatical cycles, and jubilees.
sessions.prompt: What does this grouping show?
answers: One calendar boundary can organize several related fields without making every field identical.
Tishrei makes the other new years disappear.
Every date in the Mishnah serves only one purpose.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Mishnah groups functions while still keeping its categories visible.

sessions.title: A calendar boundary can be disputed
sessions.hebrew: בית שמאי אומרים באחד בשבט · בית הלל אומרים בחמשה עשר בו
sessions.translation: Beit Shammai say on the first of Shevat; Beit Hillel say on the fifteenth of it.
sessions.prompt: What does this disagreement add to the map?
answers: The tree-calendar category has a contested boundary, so both positions must be kept distinct.
All earlier categories were mistakes.
The Mishnah no longer cares about dates.
sessions.feedback: Yes. A dispute changes the boundary in one category; it does not erase the structure of the whole Mishnah.

sessions.title: Gemara asks what the date is for
sessions.translation: For kings, for what legal purpose?
sessions.prompt: What is the Gemara asking?
answers: What practical legal function is served by counting a king’s years from a fixed date.
Which king first celebrated the festival.
Whether a new year has any categories.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara turns a stated calendar category into a question about its function.

sessions.title: A fixed date makes records intelligible
sessions.translation: Rav Ḥisda said: For documents.
sessions.prompt: What does this answer contribute?
answers: It gives a public-record function for the fixed dating convention.
It turns the Mishnah into personal financial advice.
It says documents are unrelated to calendar counting.
sessions.feedback: Right. The answer supplies the institutional function that makes the category intelligible.

sessions.title: Keep category, boundary, and function together
sessions.translation: Count · domain · date · purpose.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for an unfamiliar source that gives several dates?
answers: Name the categories, connect each date to its domain, then ask what function the boundary serves.
Choose the most familiar date and ignore the rest.
Treat every date as a separate personal instruction.
sessions.feedback: You can now read calendar language as a structured legal map while keeping the study text distinct from practical guidance.

sessions.title: Recall the Gemara’s move
sessions.translation: For what legal purpose?
sessions.prompt: When Gemara asks “for what legal purpose?”, what should you look for next?
answers: The function the stated rule or category performs in its source setting.
A personal instruction for today.
A reason to disregard the Mishnah’s wording.
sessions.feedback: Good. This question signals that the Gemara is seeking the function of a stated category.

sanhedrin.title: Ask why a Mishnah says more than it seems to need.
sanhedrin.intro: Sanhedrin opens with court categories and a repeated number. The Gemara treats that repetition as deliberate: first map the category and its examples, then ask what the wording is doing.

sessions.title: A Mishnah begins with a category
sessions.translation: Cases concerning monetary law are adjudicated by three.
sessions.prompt: What does this first phrase give a reader?
answers: A broad case category together with the court number the Mishnah assigns to it.
A personal instruction for resolving a present-day dispute.
A claim that every legal matter is identical.
sessions.feedback: Right. Begin by separating the field named from the number attached to it.

sessions.title: The Mishnah specifies cases
sessions.translation: Cases of robbery and personal injury are adjudicated by three.
sessions.prompt: How should a careful reader relate this phrase to the category that came before it?
answers: As named cases that appear to sit inside the broader monetary-law category, with the same stated number.
As proof that robbery and injury cannot be monetary cases.
As a new personal ruling that replaces the Mishnah’s opening phrase.
sessions.feedback: Good. The category and the named cases are not yet the same kind of statement; their relation is exactly what the Gemara will probe.

sessions.title: A repeated detail can create a question
sessions.hebrew: אַטּוּ גְּזֵילוֹת וַחֲבָלוֹת לָאו דִּינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת נִינְהוּ?
sessions.translation: Are robbery and personal-injury cases not monetary-law cases?
sessions.prompt: What pressure does the Gemara put on the Mishnah’s wording?
answers: If the named cases already belong to the broad category, why does the Mishnah specify them separately?
Whether robbery and injury are ordinary Hebrew words.
Whether a learner may decide a court case from this page.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara assumes deliberate wording and asks what the added specification accomplishes.

sessions.title: The question is about wording, not the result
sessions.translation: Are they not monetary-law cases?
sessions.prompt: Which paraphrase preserves the Gemara’s actual question?
answers: Why list robbery and injury separately if they are already cases of monetary law?
Are robbery and injury ever important subjects?
Which litigant should win a robbery case today?
sessions.feedback: Right. Keep a textual question about specification separate from any live legal conclusion.

sessions.title: The Gemara proposes a way to read the Mishnah
sessions.hebrew: מָה הֵן קָתָנֵי, מָה הֵן דִּינֵי מָמוֹנוֹת? גְּזֵילוֹת וַחֲבָלוֹת
sessions.translation: It teaches: what are these monetary-law cases? Robbery and personal-injury cases.
sessions.prompt: What does this proposal do to the Mishnah’s two phrases?
answers: It reads the second phrase as specifying which cases the first category is talking about.
It erases the first phrase as meaningless.
It turns the Mishnah into an instruction for a modern court.
sessions.feedback: Good. “What are these?” is a reading proposal: a category followed by its specification.

sessions.title: A specification can narrow a category
sessions.translation: But admissions and loans, no.
sessions.prompt: What reading habit does this limit reinforce?
answers: A broad label may be clarified or narrowed by the cases a source explicitly specifies.
A category label always includes every imaginable case without qualification.
A learner should infer a practical legal rule without further study.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A close reader tracks both what a category includes and the limits a source itself marks.

sessions.title: The Gemara grounds a case in Torah language
sessions.translation: The owner of the house shall come near the court.
sessions.prompt: What should a learner ask when the Gemara brings a Torah phrase into its explanation?
answers: What role the verse is playing in the Gemara’s account of this category, before claiming more than the source says.
Which current dispute the verse settles immediately.
Whether the verse makes the Mishnah unnecessary.
sessions.feedback: Right. Source tracing asks how a cited text functions in the argument; it is not a shortcut to practical judgment.

sessions.title: Court sources require a firm boundary
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy’s responsible role when studying Sanhedrin?
answers: Teach the Mishnah and Gemara’s textual structure while directing real legal questions to qualified authorities and appropriate institutions.
Use an ancient court text to decide a learner’s dispute.
Avoid all court texts because they can never be studied responsibly.
sessions.feedback: Correct. The seriousness of the material calls for more careful study, not simulated legal authority.

sessions.title: A category and its cases appear elsewhere
sessions.translation: There are four primary categories of damage.
sessions.prompt: What can the Sanhedrin reading habit help you do in this new Mishnah?
answers: Ask how the named categories, examples, and any shared principle relate before treating the list as a flat set of facts.
Assume every category-list means exactly what Sanhedrin means.
Skip the source because categories are only vocabulary lists.
sessions.feedback: Good transfer. Structural habits travel, while each new source still needs its own close reading.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: What are these?
