sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of מָה הֵן in a few words.
sessions.feedback: You recalled the phrase that introduces the Gemara’s category-and-specification reading.

shabbat.kicker: SECOND GATEWAY TRACTATE · CASES AND CATEGORIES
shabbat.title: Read a legal world through its cases.
shabbat.intro: Shabbat teaches a different kind of Gemara reading from Berakhot: counted cases, domains, action, responsibility, and the distinctions that make a legal category meaningful.

sessions.title: A number opens a legal field
sessions.translation: The acts of carrying out on Shabbat are two that are four.
sessions.prompt: What should this opening make a learner expect?
answers: Basic cases and related extensions that require careful sorting.
A list of four rulings, each stated once and needing no analysis.
A dispute in which two sages each count the categories differently.
sessions.feedback: A counted Mishnah signals that the learner must track categories and cases — “two that are four” promises structure to unpack, not a flat list or a machloket about arithmetic.

sessions.title: Location changes a case
sessions.translation: Inside · outside.
sessions.prompt: Why do these words matter?
answers: They distinguish domains that shape the legal case.
They tell you which of the two people owns the object.
They mark where the action is permitted and where it is forbidden.
sessions.feedback: Legal reasoning often begins by locating where an action occurs — the domains define the case itself; ownership and permission are further questions the case will raise.

sessions.title: Find what each person does
sessions.hebrew: הֶעָנִי עוֹמֵד בַּחוּץ וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת בִּפְנִים
sessions.translation: The poor person stands outside and the homeowner stands inside.
sessions.prompt: What must a learner map before deciding the outcome?
answers: Who acts, where each person stands, and what moves between domains.
Why the poor person has come to the homeowner’s window at all.
Which of the two people bears responsibility for the transfer.
sessions.feedback: Good. Case mapping keeps legal reasoning concrete — motive is not what the Mishnah tracks, and responsibility is the outcome, which the map must precede.

sessions.title: A case points toward a category
sessions.translation: Carrying out / transfer.
sessions.prompt: What is the learning task after seeing several cases?
answers: Ask what shared category organizes them and where their differences matter.
Rank the cases from the most severe violation to the least severe.
Learn each case separately, since each carries its own ruling.
sessions.feedback: A category makes several cases intelligible as part of one legal field — severity-ranking and case-by-case memorization both miss the structure that makes the field learnable.

sessions.title: Similar cases can differ
sessions.translation: This is inside · that is outside.
sessions.prompt: What kind of reasoning move is this?
answers: A distinction that explains why superficially similar cases may differ.
A compromise assigning partial liability to each of the parties.
A restatement of the two cases in the order they occurred.
sessions.feedback: Right. Legal mastery depends on seeing the feature that changes the category — the distinction re-maps the cases; it does not split liability or merely restate.

sessions.title: Study does not become a personal ruling automatically
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of this learning?
answers: Understand source structure while bringing personal practical questions to qualified guidance.
Apply the categories just learned to resolve one’s own Shabbat questions.
Study the concepts in the abstract while avoiding practical topics.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning includes knowing the boundary between text study and personal decision — self-application and topic-avoidance are the two tempting ways to lose it.

sessions.title: One tractate, more than one subject
sessions.hebrew: לֹא יֵשֵׁב אָדָם לִפְנֵי הַסַּפָּר סָמוּךְ לַמִּנְחָה
sessions.translation: A person should not sit before the barber close to the time of Mincha.
sessions.prompt: Mishnah 1:1 discussed domains and transfer. What does the very next Mishnah do?
answers: Move to a completely different topic — timing restrictions before the afternoon prayer — while remaining in the same tractate.
Apply the domains framework of 1:1 to the barber’s shop as a new case.
Introduce the exception that limits the transfer rules just taught.
sessions.feedback: Right. A tractate is organized by broad subject, not one continuous argument — the barber Mishnah is neither a new domains case nor an exception; it is a genuine topic shift.

sessions.title: A timing rule has its own concern
sessions.translation: Lest he forget and not pray.
sessions.prompt: What kind of concern explains this pre-Mincha restriction?
answers: A concern that an absorbing activity could cause someone to miss a fixed prayer time entirely.
A concern that haircutting itself is inappropriate so close to a sacred hour.
A concern that the visit would run past nightfall and into Shabbat.
sessions.feedback: Good. The stated reason is forgetting to pray — not the dignity of the hour, and not Shabbat at all. Reading the Gemara’s own reason beats guessing a plausible one.

sessions.title: Move from Shabbat to Eruvin
sessions.translation: An alleyway that is high.
sessions.prompt: What Shabbat skill transfers to this new source?
answers: Map the physical case and ask which feature creates the legal category.
Apply the inside/outside domain labels from Shabbat 1:1 to the alleyway.
Look for the poor person and homeowner in the new case’s roles.
sessions.feedback: You can carry case mapping into a new legal world — the skill transfers, but Shabbat’s specific labels and actors do not; that is exactly what makes it transfer rather than repetition.

sessions.title: Read the case before the ruling
sessions.translation: Poor person · homeowner · inside · outside.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move?
answers: Map people, domains, action, and relation before deciding what category is at stake.
Recall the ruling for this case from the earlier lesson and confirm it.
Identify which of the four terms is the legally decisive one.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a case-based sugya with a concrete map — recalling old conclusions and hunting one decisive word are both faster and both wrong.

sessions.title: Recall the source roles
sessions.translation: Poor person · homeowner.
sessions.prompt: Which pair organizes the opening case?
answers: Poor person and homeowner.
Barber and person praying Mincha.
Two witnesses and a court.
sessions.feedback: A source map becomes durable when you can recognize its essential actors in the source itself.

shevuot.kicker: NEZIKIN SOURCE TRAIL · PATTERN AND DERIVATION
shevuot.title: Read a repeated pattern without flattening its subject.
shevuot.intro: Shevuot opens “two that are four,” a form already familiar from Shabbat. Learn what the pattern predicts, then see how oaths have their own source, expansion, and limits.

sessions.title: Two that are four
sessions.translation: Oaths: two that are four.
sessions.prompt: What should this opening make a reader expect?
answers: A basic pair whose cases will expand into a larger counted field.
A single ruling with no categories to unpack.
Two sages disagreeing about how many oaths exist.
sessions.feedback: Right. The number is a map signal: look for the basic categories and their extensions.

sessions.title: The same form appeared in Shabbat
sessions.translation: The acts of carrying out on Shabbat are two that are four.
sessions.prompt: What transfers from Shabbat into Shevuot?
answers: The expectation of a counted pair and extensions, not Shabbat’s particular subject matter.
The rule that every oath concerns carrying between domains.
The conclusion that identical wording makes the two legal fields identical.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A reading form can transfer while the content and stakes of the new field remain distinct.

sessions.title: Positive and negative oaths
sessions.translation: I will eat · I will not eat.
sessions.prompt: What basic pair is being named?
answers: A positive and a negative oath about a future act.
Two unrelated ways of carrying on Shabbat.
A dispute between two witnesses about a past event.
sessions.feedback: Good. Begin with the two stated cases before trying to account for all four.

sessions.title: Past language expands the field
sessions.translation: I ate · I did not eat.
sessions.prompt: How do these cases help explain “two that are four”?
answers: They extend the positive and negative pair from future language to past language.
They replace the first two cases with an unrelated set of four.
They show the opening number was only decorative language.
sessions.feedback: Right. The count records an expansion of a stated pair, not a random list.

sessions.title: A source category is not personal advice
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of this source trail?
answers: Read its categories and derivation while bringing personal vow questions to qualified guidance.
Apply the cases directly to personal commitments without further guidance.
Avoid noticing the source’s practical stakes altogether.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning includes recognizing when textual literacy is not practical decision-making.

sessions.title: Read a new counted opening
sessions.translation: Two · four · category · extension.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first move when a new Mishnah opens with a number?
answers: Name the stated pair, ask how it expands, and keep the new field’s subject distinct.
Assume every repeated count uses the same cases as Shabbat.
Memorize the number before looking for the categories behind it.
sessions.feedback: You can now use a repeated Mishnaic form as a reading aid without confusing one tractate with another.

sotah.kicker: NASHIM SOURCE TRAIL - TESTIMONY, RITUAL, UNCERTAINTY
sotah.title: Read evidence and ritual without collapsing uncertainty.
sotah.intro: Sotah asks how a formal warning, witnesses, seclusion, and a defined ritual procedure shape what can responsibly be inferred. Learn the source’s sequence before drawing conclusions.

sessions.title: A warning is not yet proof
sessions.translation: A warning is made in the presence of two witnesses.
sessions.prompt: What does the opening requirement establish?
answers: The warning is a formal evidentiary act requiring two witnesses, not merely a private suspicion.
Any rumor automatically begins the ritual.
The witnesses decide the outcome before the procedure begins.
sessions.feedback: Right. Sotah begins by specifying the evidence needed even to initiate the formal process.

sessions.title: Two stages carry different work
sessions.translation: Warning and seclusion.
sessions.prompt: Why keep these stages distinct?
answers: The warning creates a formal condition, while subsequent seclusion supplies a different procedural fact.
The two terms are interchangeable names for one accusation.
Seclusion alone proves guilt without any prior warning.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Mishnah builds a sequence; each stage has its own evidentiary role.

sessions.title: What can witnesses establish?
sessions.translation: There is no witness against her.
sessions.prompt: What is the careful question to ask about testimony?
answers: Identify what the witnesses saw and which procedural condition that observation can establish.
Treat every witness statement as proof of the entire underlying event.
Ignore the witness requirement once the ritual is mentioned.
sessions.feedback: Good. Evidence has scope: a witness can establish a condition without supplying every conclusion.

sessions.title: The ritual has ordered steps
sessions.translation: The bitter waters.
sessions.prompt: Why does the ritual sequence matter for reading the source?
answers: The ordered acts and materials define the textual procedure; they are not interchangeable symbols.
Any meaningful substitute preserves the same legal procedure.
The ritual details are later decoration with no interpretive force.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Sotah trains attention to how material and sequence carry the procedure.

sessions.title: What if the evidence is incomplete?
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: What kind of problem does the Gemara raise around uncertain evidence?
answers: It asks how the ritual framework responds when the required facts or testimony do not line up cleanly.
It assumes uncertainty has no effect on the process.
It replaces the source with a modern intuition about trust.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Gemara makes evidentiary uncertainty an explicit question rather than silently resolving it.

sessions.title: Suspicion is not a verdict
sessions.translation: She secluded herself and there is no witness.
sessions.prompt: What boundary follows from the source?
answers: Distinguish suspicion, witnessed conditions, and the ritual’s procedural result instead of treating them as identical.
A suspicion is enough to announce guilt publicly.
The absence of a witness proves the accusation false.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The text preserves uncertainty and channels it through a defined procedure.

sessions.title: Sensitive law needs careful boundaries
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · not to issue a ruling.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy’s responsible stance?
answers: Study testimony and ritual historically while directing any personal, pastoral, or legal concern to qualified authorities.
Apply the ancient procedure directly to a contemporary relationship.
Avoid the tractate because its subject is difficult.
sessions.feedback: Serious study can hold difficult sources with precision without pretending to replace guidance.

sessions.title: Map a disputed evidentiary case
sessions.translation: Warning · witnesses · seclusion · uncertainty.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for an unfamiliar Sotah passage?
answers: List the warning, witness requirement, subsequent condition, ritual step, and remaining uncertainty before drawing a conclusion.
Begin with a verdict based on the emotional plausibility of the story.
Treat every element as one undifferentiated accusation.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Sotah through evidence, procedure, uncertainty, and responsible boundaries.

sukkah.title: Read a legal world built from physical validity.
sukkah.intro: Sukkah teaches how a measurement becomes a ruling, how a ruling invites a reason, and how a distinction can show that two seemingly conflicting sources are each correct about a different case.

sessions.title: What is being measured?
sessions.hebrew: סֻכָּה שֶׁהִיא גְבוֹהָה לְמַעְלָה מֵעֶשְׂרִים אַמָּה
sessions.translation: A sukkah that is higher than twenty cubits.
sessions.prompt: What concrete feature does the Mishnah place before the reader?
answers: The height of a sukkah.
The time of a festival meal.
The owner of a field.
sessions.feedback: Good. Begin with the physical case before asking why the measure matters.

sessions.title: A measurement is a boundary
sessions.translation: Higher than twenty cubits.
sessions.prompt: What job does this measurement phrase do in the sentence?
answers: It defines the specific boundary condition the ruling depends on.
It names the builder of the sukkah.
It has no effect on the ruling that follows.
sessions.feedback: Right. A measurement is not decoration; it creates the boundary a Mishnah will reason about.

sessions.title: Know what you are measuring
sessions.translation: Sukkah / booth.
sessions.prompt: Before applying any rule, what must a learner identify about the structure itself?
answers: What physical feature is being measured and why that feature might matter halakhically.
The name of the festival the structure is used for.
Whether the structure has ever been rebuilt.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Naming the object precisely is the first step before reasoning about its validity.

sessions.title: What does the Mishnah say?
sessions.translation: It is invalid.
sessions.prompt: What kind of statement is this, following the case just described?
answers: A ruling about the described case.
A question about a verse.
A description of a custom.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Mishnah’s short ruling gives the Gemara something precise to investigate.

sessions.title: What comes next?
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: What productive question does this phrase invite after a bare ruling like פְּסוּלָה?
answers: Why does this height affect the validity of the sukkah?
Who built the first sukkah?
Which word is easiest to translate?
sessions.feedback: Right. A measurement becomes a Gemara question when the reader asks what principle explains it.

sessions.title: Two sources, two cases
sessions.translation: This is in one case; that is in another.
sessions.prompt: If two sources seemed to disagree about a sukkah’s valid height, what move would a careful reader look for first?
answers: A distinction showing the sources describe genuinely different cases, not a real disagreement.
A decision to discard one of the two sources.
A translation exercise unrelated to the disagreement.
sessions.feedback: Good. Legal mastery depends on seeing the feature that changes the category.

sessions.short: A new case: an unusual shape
sessions.title: When is a covering not a roof?
sessions.translation: One who makes it like a kind of hut, with sloped, roofless sides.
sessions.prompt: After the height measurement, what new kind of case does the Mishnah introduce?
answers: A structural question about whether a sukkah with no flat roof, only sloped sides, can be valid.
A repeat of the same height rule in different words.
An unrelated case about a different festival.
sessions.feedback: Right. Height was one boundary condition; shape turns out to be a second, independent one.

sessions.title: What counts as a roof?
sessions.translation: Rabbi Eliezer invalidates it … and the Sages validate it.
sessions.prompt: Rabbi Eliezer’s stated reason is that the structure lacks a roof. What does this dispute reveal about defining a sukkah?
answers: Two real positions differ on whether a sukkah’s covering must be a flat, distinct roof, or whether sloped walls that meet overhead can count as covering too.
The Sages secretly agree with Rabbi Eliezer but phrase it differently.
The dispute has nothing to do with what makes a sukkah valid.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A named reason (“it has no roof”) lets you see precisely what concept the two sides are actually contesting.

sessions.title: Condition, then consequence
sessions.translation: Higher than twenty cubits … it is invalid.
sessions.prompt: This is the same skeleton read earlier in Mishnah grammar. What should transfer from Sukkah to any new tractate?
answers: A described case or measurement followed directly by its practical consequence.
A question followed by an unrelated answer.
Two facts placed together by coincidence.
sessions.feedback: Once you can name a sentence’s skeleton, it becomes visible across many different Mishnayot.

sessions.title: Map the case on your own
sessions.translation: Sukkah · higher than twenty cubits · it is invalid.
sessions.prompt: What is the first independent-reading move with this case?
answers: Identify the structure, its measurement, and the ruling that follows before asking why.
Guess the ruling from the first word alone.
Assume the case has already been fully explained.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a measure-and-validity sugya with a concrete map.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: What kind of question does this phrase introduce?
answers: A question seeking the reason for a rule.
A question naming the person in a case.
A question setting the calendar date of a practice.
sessions.feedback: You can recognize a reason-question and distinguish it from questions about people or timing.

taanit.kicker: MOED SOURCE TRAIL · TIMING AND REASON
taanit.title: Read a timing dispute as an argument.
taanit.intro: Taanit opens by asking when rain is mentioned in prayer. Follow two positions, the concern that challenges one of them, and the Gemara’s question about why this tractate begins here.

sessions.title: When does the mention begin?
sessions.translation: From when do we mention the might of the rains?
sessions.prompt: What kind of problem opens the tractate?
answers: A question about when a named source practice begins.
A report of current weather.
A final ruling without a question.
sessions.feedback: Right. The source opens with a timing question, so expect positions and reasons.

sessions.title: Rabbi Eliezer begins earlier
sessions.hebrew: רבי אליעזר אומר מיום טוב הראשון של חג
sessions.translation: Rabbi Eliezer says: From the first festival day.
sessions.prompt: What must a reader preserve?
answers: This is one position with a specific starting point.
It is automatically the only view in the Mishnah.
The festival date is unrelated to the question.
sessions.feedback: Good. Begin by attaching the speaker to the claim.

sessions.title: Rabbi Yehoshua begins later
sessions.hebrew: רבי יהושע אומר מיום טוב האחרון של חג
sessions.translation: Rabbi Yehoshua says: From the last festival day.
sessions.prompt: What makes this a real disagreement?
answers: The two voices assign different starting points to the same practice.
They discuss unrelated topics.
The later date erases the first position from the source.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Keep the shared question and differing answers in view.

sessions.title: A timing claim has a concern behind it
sessions.hebrew: הואיל ואין הגשמים אלא סימן קללה בחג
sessions.translation: Since rain during the festival is only a sign of a curse.
sessions.prompt: What work does this line do?
answers: It supplies a reason that challenges beginning the mention at the start of the festival.
It gives personal weather advice.
It removes the need to map the disagreement.
sessions.feedback: Right. The source argues from the relation between the timing and the festival context.

sessions.title: Mentioning is not the same as requesting
sessions.hebrew: אף אני לא אמרתי לשאול אלא להזכיר
sessions.translation: I did not say to request, but only to mention.
sessions.prompt: What move does this reply make?
answers: It distinguishes two related practices rather than denying the concern.
It abandons the timing question.
It gives a modern prayer instruction.
sessions.feedback: Good. A distinction can preserve part of a claim while narrowing what is actually at issue.

sessions.title: Why does this tractate begin here?
sessions.hebrew: וליתני התם? מאי שנא דשבקיה עד הכא?
sessions.translation: Let it be taught there; what is different that it was left until here?
sessions.prompt: What is the Gemara asking about?
answers: Why this topic is placed in Taanit rather than where a related prayer topic appeared earlier.
Which modern community should follow which date.
Whether the Mishnah has any structure.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara treats editorial placement as a question worth explaining.

sessions.title: Read timing without flattening it
sessions.translation: Time · voice · reason · distinction.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new timing dispute?
answers: State the shared question, map each voice, locate the reason, and watch for distinctions.
Choose a date before reading the reasons.
Treat the source as direct personal guidance.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a timing dispute as a structured argument, not a bare list of dates.

tamid.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · ORDER, ROLE, DAILY SERVICE
tamid.title: Read the daily Temple service as an ordered system.
tamid.intro: Tamid follows the service from the watch before dawn through preparation, roles, sequence, and the public offering. Learn how repeated order carries purpose.

sessions.title: A service that begins before dawn
sessions.translation: house of the hearth · priests · service
sessions.prompt: What does the opening Mishnah make visible?
answers: The Temple service depends on an organized watch: people, place, and time are arranged before the public offering begins.
The opening describes a guarded sleeping arrangement whose only purpose is comfort, with no ritual schedule or assigned readiness.
Any priest may begin any service whenever he arrives, because the opening watch imposes no order on the day.
sessions.feedback: Right. Tamid opens with a watch system: readiness and assigned roles make the public service possible.

sessions.title: Order is part of the law
sessions.hebrew: terumat hadeshen · hatavat hanerot · korban tamid
sessions.translation: removal of ashes · tending the lamps · continual offering
sessions.prompt: Why does the source narrate the steps in order?
answers: Sequence teaches that the service is a coordinated chain, where timing and precedence carry legal meaning.
Sequence is mostly decorative: the actions may be exchanged whenever a participant prefers, because precedence adds no information.
Only the final offering matters, so the earlier preparation and tending can be omitted without changing what the source teaches.
sessions.feedback: Good. Tamid makes order itself an object of study: preparation, tending, and offering belong to a disciplined chain.

sessions.title: Who does what?
sessions.translation: priests · Levites · appointed representatives
sessions.prompt: What should a reader ask when several groups appear?
answers: Which role belongs to which group, and how those roles cooperate without collapsing into one undifferentiated service.
Whether all participants perform identical tasks, with role names serving only as interchangeable labels for one shared duty.
Whether role names are merely titles with no practical function, even though the source assigns different groups to the service.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The service becomes legible when each participant’s task and relationship to the whole are kept distinct.

sessions.title: Routine and meaning
sessions.translation: intention · order · honor
sessions.prompt: What distinction should remain visible?
answers: A repeated routine can carry purpose and honor; regularity does not make the service empty or mechanical.
A routine has meaning only when it is improvised, so any repeated order must be treated as spiritually empty.
Honor replaces the need for an ordered procedure, because a sincere intention makes the sequence itself irrelevant.
sessions.feedback: Right. Tamid trains the reader to see meaning through faithful order rather than opposing routine and significance.

sessions.title: Why this order?
sessions.translation: what is the reason · order of service
sessions.prompt: What does a Gemara source-question invite here?
answers: Ask which textual or traditional reason explains the sequence, role, or honor described by the Mishnah.
Replace the source’s order with whatever seems efficient today, without asking how the Mishnah or tradition itself explains the sequence.
Assume the sequence needs no explanation because it is familiar, and treat the Gemara’s question as a request for modern efficiency instead.
sessions.feedback: Good. A Gemara question turns the remembered order into an object of reasoning: why this step, in this place, by this role?

sessions.title: When conditions change
sessions.translation: time · place · error
sessions.prompt: What should a reader test after mapping the routine?
answers: Which conditions preserve the service’s sequence and which require a different response when time, place, or human error intervenes.
Whether every disruption erases the entire service, even when the source distinguishes a changed condition from a total collapse of the order.
Whether conditions can be ignored once the participants are named, because roles alone determine the service regardless of time, place, or error.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Scope work asks how a stable order responds to changed conditions without losing its defining structure.

sessions.title: Study is not reenactment
sessions.translation: to learn · to understand · to ask
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of Tamid sources?
answers: Study the ancient service as historical and textual knowledge, while distinguishing it from present-day observance and practice.
Treat the ancient Temple schedule as a current ritual instruction that learners should reproduce as though the historical setting and authority were still present.
Avoid the service details because the Temple setting is historical, as though a source cannot be studied carefully once its original practice has ended.
sessions.feedback: Serious study preserves both precision and boundaries: we can learn the service deeply without pretending to perform it today.

sessions.title: Map a service sequence
sessions.translation: order · role · time · honor
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new Tamid passage?
answers: Name the stage, assign the roles, mark the timing and purpose, then test how the order responds to changed conditions.
Start with the final offering and infer every earlier role afterward, allowing the conclusion to stand in for the sequence and its assigned participants.
Treat sequence, role, and purpose as interchangeable labels, because distinguishing them would add detail without helping a reader map the passage.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Tamid by tracking order, role, time, purpose, and responsible historical boundaries.

tefillah.title: Learn to navigate prayer from the inside.
tefillah.intro: Read prayer as Hebrew language, literary structure, biblical reception, rabbinic practice, and intentional address. The aim is understanding and participation—not performance or coercion.

sessions.title: A service has a shape
sessions.translation: Shema · prayer · thanksgiving.
sessions.prompt: What is the most useful first way to enter an unfamiliar service?
answers: Identify the major sections and ask what each is meant to do.
Learn the historical period in which each section was composed.
Master the Hebrew of the opening section before going further.
sessions.feedback: Good. Structure gives a learner orientation before fluency — history and vocabulary both matter, but the map of functions is what makes a service navigable.

sessions.title: The Shema begins in Torah
sessions.hebrew: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד
sessions.translation: Hear, O Israel: the Lord is our God, the Lord is one.
sessions.prompt: What does this source contribute to the service?
answers: A foundational biblical declaration that the liturgy receives and repeats.
A blessing formula composed by the sages for daily recitation.
A petition asking God to unify a scattered community.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Siddur often brings biblical language into recurring communal practice — this line is Torah received, not rabbinic composition, and declaration, not petition.

sessions.title: A blessing can begin with praise
sessions.translation: Blessed are You, Lord.
sessions.prompt: What kind of liturgical move is this formula making?
answers: Addressing God in a language of blessing and praise.
Requesting that God grant what the prayer is about to ask.
Declaring a biblical verse fulfilled in the present moment.
sessions.feedback: Good. Naming the move helps the learner hear what a section is doing — baruch atah opens in praise; the asking, when it comes, is a different move.

sessions.title: Some prayer asks
sessions.translation: Grant us knowledge, understanding, and discernment.
sessions.prompt: What makes this a petition?
answers: It asks for a human need in direct address to God.
It praises God as the source of all human knowledge.
It thanks God for understanding already received.
sessions.feedback: Right. Petition is one distinct mode of prayer — chanenu asks. The same theme could be praised or thanked, and the Amidah does both elsewhere; the verb tells you which.

sessions.title: Some prayer gives thanks
sessions.translation: We give thanks to You.
sessions.prompt: What is the central action of this phrase?
answers: Expressing gratitude.
Requesting protection.
Confessing wrongdoing.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Modim gives thanks — though the same root can carry confession elsewhere in the liturgy, which is why reading the move matters.

sessions.title: Prayer becomes a question
sessions.translation: The patriarchs instituted the prayers.
sessions.prompt: What kind of question does this Gemara statement invite?
answers: How prayer’s times and origins are understood and argued in rabbinic tradition.
Which patriarch composed which words of the daily service.
Whether prayer existed at all before the patriarchs instituted it.
sessions.feedback: Good. Gemara turns familiar practice into a source-based discussion — the sugya debates origins and times, not authorship of wording, and it offers a second view (the sacrifices) too.

sessions.title: Words and attention both matter
sessions.hebrew: הַקּוֹרֵא אֶת שְׁמַע וְלֹא הִשְׁמִיעַ לְאָזְנוֹ
sessions.translation: One who recites Shema but does not make it audible to their ear.
sessions.prompt: What kind of study question can this open?
answers: How words, attention, voice, and practice interact in the experience of prayer.
Whether silent reading counts as recitation for every obligation.
What volume the halakha requires for each part of the service.
sessions.feedback: Right. Tefillah joins language, embodied practice, and intention — the Mishnah opens that whole field, while the two practical questions belong to qualified guidance.

sessions.title: Understanding prayer is not a ruling
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: You can now name praise, petition, and thanksgiving in the Siddur. What is Jewish Learning Academy’s appropriate role here?
answers: Help learners read and understand the liturgy while directing practical questions about prayer obligations to qualified guidance.
Provide the sources on prayer obligations so learners can resolve their own practical questions.
Keep practical topics out of view so that no practical question can arise from study.
sessions.feedback: Moral seriousness includes being clear that understanding what prayer means is not the same as resolving a practical question — self-psak and avoidance both erase that line.

sessions.title: Read the function before the translation
sessions.translation: Blessed · grant us · we give thanks.
sessions.prompt: What map should a learner recognize?
answers: Praise, petition, and thanksgiving are different forms of address within prayer.
Three stages of one request, building from opening to close.
Three names for the same act of blessing, varied for style.
sessions.feedback: You can now enter a new prayer section by asking what kind of address its language performs — three moves, not one move three times.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.translation: We give thanks to You.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of this phrase in a few words.
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

temurah.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · SUBSTITUTION, DESIGNATION, CONSEQUENCE
temurah.title: Read the legal paradox of a forbidden substitution.
temurah.intro: Temurah follows what happens when one consecrated offering is named in place of another. Track the designation, the prohibition, the consequence, and the limits of the rule.

sessions.title: One offering named for another
sessions.translation: substitution · consecrated object · offering
sessions.prompt: What pressure does the opening case create?
answers: It asks what happens when someone attempts to exchange one consecrated offering for another.
It says consecrated animals can be traded like ordinary property.
It treats the attempted exchange as having no legal significance at all.
sessions.feedback: Right. Temurah begins with a prohibited substitution attempt and asks what legal status follows from it.

sessions.title: The act is not permitted
sessions.translation: he shall not exchange it · good for bad
sessions.prompt: What should a reader identify before tracking the result?
answers: That the Torah forbids exchanging one consecrated animal for another.
That every exchange is permitted if the replacement is more valuable.
That the prohibition applies only to ordinary property.
sessions.feedback: Good. The prohibition is the starting category; the later consequence does not make the act permissible.

sessions.title: Designation changes the map
sessions.translation: consecration · designation · animal
sessions.prompt: Why does the source track which animal was designated?
answers: Because the legal consequence depends on the consecrated status of the original and the proposed substitute.
Because designation is only a descriptive label with no legal force.
Because the source treats every animal as already consecrated.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. A careful reading preserves the designation facts before deciding what consequence follows.

sessions.title: Forbidden does not mean ineffective
sessions.translation: prohibition · takes effect · sanctity
sessions.prompt: What distinction should remain visible?
answers: The substitution can be forbidden while still producing a legally recognized consequence.
If an act is forbidden, it can never change any legal status.
A legal effect makes the original act automatically permitted.
sessions.feedback: Right. Temurah teaches a crucial legal distinction: prohibition and legal effect can coexist.

sessions.title: Why does the result follow?
sessions.translation: what is the reason · from where
sessions.prompt: What does a Gemara source-question invite here?
answers: Ask which verse and interpretive principle make the attempted substitution consequential.
Replace the source with a modern rule about contracts.
Ignore the wording because the result is only a practical custom.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Gemara presses past the paradox to identify the scriptural basis for the consequence.

sessions.title: What transfers, and what remains?
sessions.translation: original · substitute · condition
sessions.prompt: What should a reader test after finding the rule?
answers: Which status attaches to the substitute and which conditions limit the rule in a new case.
Whether every proposed replacement receives the same status in every circumstance.
Whether the original offering disappears from the analysis.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Scope work asks what transfers, what remains, and which conditions qualify the consequence.

sessions.title: Historical sacrificial categories
sessions.translation: to learn · to understand · to ask
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of these substitution sources?
answers: Study their categories and reasoning as historical textual literacy, not as practical sacrificial instruction.
Treat the ancient substitution rule as a current ritual procedure.
Avoid the legal reasoning because the Temple setting is historical.
sessions.feedback: Serious study can honor the source while clearly distinguishing historical sacrificial law from present practice.

sessions.title: Map a disciplined paradox
sessions.translation: act · prohibition · consequence · boundary
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a new substitution case?
answers: Name the act, identify the prohibition, state the legal consequence, then test its boundary.
Choose the consequence first and use the prohibition only afterward.
Treat a forbidden act and an ineffective act as interchangeable.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Temurah by tracking act, prohibition, consequence, and boundary in order.

widerworld.pageTitle: Jewish Learning Academy · Wider World Arc
widerworld.kicker: WIDER WORLD ARC · LAW, REASON, AND COMPARISON
widerworld.title: Compare traditions without flattening them.
widerworld.intro: This arc begins with a Jewish source, names a question it shares with wider intellectual worlds, traces how ideas actually traveled across languages, and asks how law and philosophy each meet a wider canon.

sessions.title: A Jewish source frames the question
sessions.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
sessions.prompt: What comparative question can this open?
answers: How Jewish communities understand responsibility toward the societies in which they live.
How other ancient traditions instructed exiles to relate to foreign cities.
Whether civic responsibility is a universal value shared by all traditions.
sessions.feedback: Good. Comparison starts from a real source and a precise question — the Jewish source’s own claim comes first; the outside parallels and the universality question come after.

sessions.title: Similarity is not identity
sessions.translation: Wisdom · Torah.
sessions.prompt: What is a responsible first comparison?
answers: Ask how two traditions define a shared word or question before declaring them equivalent.
Find the tradition in which the shared word first appeared, and read outward from it.
List the similarities first, since differences only make sense against common ground.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Shared questions can lead to very different conceptual worlds — priority-hunting and similarity-first are both tempting orders that skip the definitions.

sessions.title: Ideas travel through languages
sessions.translation: Arabic · Hebrew · Latin.
sessions.prompt: What does this linguistic map make possible?
answers: Study translation, exchange, disagreement, and adaptation across intellectual worlds.
Identify which language preserved each idea in its most original form.
Track how Hebrew absorbed vocabulary from the surrounding languages.
sessions.feedback: Jewish thinkers often worked in multilingual intellectual settings — the map opens the whole traffic of ideas, not just originality contests or loanword lists.

sessions.title: Practice meets public life
sessions.translation: Law · community · polity.
sessions.prompt: What kind of question belongs here?
answers: How covenantal legal reasoning addresses institutions, commerce, medicine, or public responsibility.
Which areas of public life halakha leaves entirely to the state’s law.
How Jewish communities kept their legal system separate from civic life.
sessions.feedback: This is a place where Halakha and wider civic worlds meet without becoming identical — neither a division of territory nor a wall, but reasoned engagement.

sessions.title: A wider canon, a shared vocabulary
sessions.translation: Reason · prophecy.
sessions.prompt: What is a careful learning question here?
answers: How Jewish thinkers relate reason and revelation while engaging wider philosophical vocabularies.
Which Jewish thinkers accepted philosophy and which rejected it outright.
Whether reason or revelation carries the final authority when they conflict.
sessions.feedback: Good. Dialogue includes reception, disagreement, and creative reinterpretation — the accept/reject sorting and the final-authority question flatten a subtler conversation.

sessions.title: Read it again, with more in view
sessions.translation: Seek the welfare of the city.
sessions.prompt: Reading the verse again with law and reason in view, what comparative question opens?
answers: How different legal and philosophical traditions each ground civic responsibility, and where they genuinely diverge.
Whether the verse anticipated the legal principle that the law of the land is law.
How the verse’s instruction compares with the civic duties Rome asked of its subjects.
sessions.feedback: Right. A source can be reread productively once you have more categories to bring to it — the grounding question is wider than anticipation-hunting or a single Rome comparison.

sessions.title: A History move, a comparative question
sessions.translation: Source · interpretation · evidence.
sessions.prompt: This map comes from History study. How does it help compare a Jewish and a non-Jewish source?
answers: By separating what a source says from how it has been interpreted and what evidence supports that interpretation.
By establishing which of the two sources rests on the older textual tradition.
By keeping each source inside its own context so the two are never confused.
sessions.feedback: A reasoning move built for one subject can sharpen comparative reading in another — the map enables comparison; age-ranking and strict separation each avoid it.

sessions.title: Compare without flattening
sessions.translation: Source · context · comparison.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible order of comparative learning?
answers: Read each source in context, name the shared question, then compare similarity and difference.
Compare the sources line by line first, then supply context for the differences found.
Name the shared question first, then read each source for its answer to that question.
sessions.feedback: You can now compare traditions with curiosity, accuracy, and respect for difference — context precedes comparison, and even the shared question must wait for the sources to speak.

sessions.title: Recall, don’t just recognize
sessions.hebrew: וּדְרְשׁוּ אֶת־שְׁלוֹם הָעִיר אֲשֶׁר הִגְלֵיתִי אֶתְכֶם שָׁמָּה
sessions.translation: Seek the welfare of the city to which I have exiled you.
sessions.prompt: Type the English meaning of the first four Hebrew words — the instruction itself — in a few words.
acceptable: seek the welfare of the city
seek the peace of the city
and seek the welfare of the city
and seek the peace of the city
seek the wellbeing of the city
sessions.feedback: Typing an answer from memory is a stronger test of durable mastery than recognizing it among choices.

yevamot.kicker: NASHIM SOURCE TRAIL - FAMILY LAW, OBLIGATION, EXEMPTION
yevamot.title: Read family-law categories through obligation and release.
yevamot.intro: Yevamot asks how kinship categories shape levirate obligation, exemptions, prohibited relationships, and the procedure of chalitzah. Learn to map the source before drawing modern conclusions.

sessions.title: A list can carry a legal mechanism
sessions.translation: Fifteen women exempt their co-wives and rival co-wives.
sessions.prompt: What should a reader notice first?
answers: The counted list is organized around an exemption mechanism, not merely a family tree.
The Mishnah treats every family relationship as identical.
The list is only a narrative opening with no legal work.
sessions.feedback: Right. Yevamot opens with a count whose structure tells you how the exemption operates.

sessions.title: What does levirate obligation require?
sessions.translation: Levirate marriage or the release ceremony.
sessions.prompt: Why identify both possible paths?
answers: The source presents a defined obligation with two legally recognized ways its relationship can be resolved.
The two terms are interchangeable modern labels with no distinction.
Only marriage matters; the release ceremony is decorative.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Yevamot asks the learner to keep yibbum and chalitzah distinct while seeing how both address the obligation.

sessions.title: Why can a relationship exempt another?
sessions.translation: They exempt their co-wives.
sessions.prompt: What is the legal effect of the counted relationships?
answers: A prohibited relationship can block the levirate bond and thereby exempt related women from the same obligation.
Any difficult relationship automatically creates a new marriage.
The exemption applies only because the family members disagree.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Mishnah builds a precise chain from prohibited kinship to exemption.

sessions.title: Not every prohibited relationship has the same scope
sessions.translation: Forbidden kinship relationships.
sessions.prompt: What does careful reading require?
answers: Track which relationship is prohibited, to whom, and whether the prohibition affects the levirate obligation.
Collapse all prohibitions into one universal rule.
Ignore the relationship category once the word prohibited appears.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Yevamot is a study in how relationship categories carry different legal consequences.

sessions.title: What is the source of the exemption?
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: What kind of question is the Gemara asking?
answers: It asks how the Torah source and the Mishnah mechanism fit together, including the scope of the exemption.
It assumes the Mishnah needs no source or explanation.
It replaces textual reasoning with a judgment about family custom.
sessions.feedback: Right. The Gemara turns the list into a source-and-scope problem.

sessions.title: Chalitzah is a procedure, not a metaphor
sessions.translation: She removes his shoe before him.
sessions.prompt: Why attend to the procedure?
answers: Concrete acts, witnesses, and sequence determine whether the release has occurred in the source’s legal frame.
The physical acts are symbols that can be rearranged freely.
Procedure matters only for modern ceremony, not for the text.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Yevamot trains the reader to see how a procedure carries legal force.

sessions.title: Family law sources need careful boundaries
sessions.translation: Historical study, not legal advice.
sessions.prompt: What is Jewish Learning Academy’s responsible stance?
answers: Study the categories historically and distinguish them from present-day legal, pastoral, or personal advice.
Apply an ancient family-law rule automatically to a contemporary person.
Avoid difficult sources because their social setting is unfamiliar.
sessions.feedback: Serious learning preserves historical precision and protects learners from mistaking study for advice.

sessions.title: Map an unfamiliar family-law case
sessions.translation: Relationship · prohibition · obligation · exemption.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for an unfamiliar Yevamot case?
answers: Identify the relationship category, the obligation, any prohibition, the exemption mechanism, and the procedure that resolves it.
Begin with a verdict based on modern family expectations.
Treat every relationship as either marriage or no relationship.
sessions.feedback: You can now read Yevamot through relationship categories, obligation, exemption, and careful boundaries.

yoma.title: Read a procedure as a reasoned safeguard.
yoma.intro: Yoma begins with preparation for the High Priest’s Temple service. Study how a Mishnah maps a role, a procedure, and a concern; how a disagreement tests the limits of precaution; and how the Gemara seeks a source. This is source study, not practical instruction.

sessions.title: Preparation is the opening case
sessions.hebrew: שבעת ימים קודם יום הכפורים מפרישין כהן גדול מביתו
sessions.translation: Seven days before Yom Kippur, they remove the High Priest from his house.
sessions.prompt: What does this opening line first establish?
answers: A procedure of preparation before a defined service.
A personal instruction for every learner before a fast.
A narrative with no institutional setting.
sessions.feedback: Correct. Begin with the procedure, its actor, and the service it prepares for.

sessions.title: One role, one institutional task
sessions.translation: High Priest.
sessions.prompt: Why does naming this role matter to the case map?
answers: The procedure is assigned to a particular Temple role, not described as a universal practice.
It tells us that every priest performs the entire service.
It replaces the need to read the rest of the Mishnah.
sessions.feedback: Right. Legal and ritual sources often turn on who is responsible for a task.

sessions.title: A replacement makes the concern visible
sessions.hebrew: ומתקינין לו כהן אחר תחתיו שמא יארע בו פסול
sessions.translation: They prepare another priest in his place, lest a disqualification occur to him.
sessions.prompt: What does the replacement show about the procedure?
answers: It addresses the risk that the assigned priest may be unable to perform the service.
It proves the first priest is unimportant.
It cancels the preparation requirement.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. Read the second appointment as a safeguard tied to a stated concern.

sessions.title: A precaution can be extended
sessions.hebrew: רבי יהודה אומר אף אשה אחרת מתקינין לו
sessions.translation: Rabbi Yehuda says: They even prepare another wife for him.
sessions.prompt: What kind of move does Rabbi Yehuda make?
answers: He extends the precaution to another concern within the same case.
He changes the topic to an unrelated festival.
He supplies the final answer to every later question.
sessions.feedback: Good. Keep the base procedure and the added concern distinct.

sessions.title: An argument about endless precautions
sessions.translation: If so, there is no end to the matter.
sessions.prompt: What is the Rabbis’ response doing?
answers: It argues that an open-ended chain of contingencies cannot itself become the rule.
It denies that any preparation is needed.
It says the High Priest will never face risk.
sessions.feedback: Right. The source teaches a transferable limit on precaution without dismissing the original concern.

sessions.title: Gemara asks where the procedure comes from
sessions.translation: From where are these matters derived?
sessions.prompt: What is the Gemara asking for?
answers: A source basis for the seven-day preparation, not merely a restatement of the Mishnah.
A new schedule for Yom Kippur.
A reason to ignore the Mishnah’s procedure.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The Gemara turns an established procedure into a question about textual derivation.

sessions.title: A verse is interpreted through two phrases
sessions.hebrew: כאשר עשה ביום הזה צוה ה׳ לעשות לכפר עליכם
sessions.translation: As was done on this day, the Lord commanded to do, to make atonement for you.
sessions.prompt: How does the Yoma passage use this verse?
answers: It reads “to do” and “to make atonement” as cues for two preparation procedures.
It treats the verse as a description unrelated to Yom Kippur.
It uses the verse to issue personal ritual instructions.
sessions.feedback: Good. A proof text has an argumentative role: the Gemara explains how its words support the procedure.

sessions.title: One preparation pattern, two services
sessions.hebrew: לעשות אלו מעשי פרה לכפר אלו מעשי יום הכפורים
sessions.translation: “To do” refers to the red-heifer procedure; “to make atonement” refers to the Yom Kippur service.
sessions.prompt: What reading move connects the two procedures?
answers: The Gemara compares how a shared verse is assigned to distinct ritual contexts.
It claims the two services are identical in every detail.
It abandons the verse after citing it.
sessions.feedback: Right. Comparison can show a shared textual pattern without flattening different contexts.

sessions.title: Read preparation without turning it into advice
sessions.translation: Preparation · concern · limit · source.
sessions.prompt: In an unfamiliar source about a preparation procedure, what is the best first map?
answers: Name the role, procedure, stated concern, any limit on precaution, and the source offered for it.
Assume the procedure tells you what to do personally.
Reduce the source to a single Hebrew word.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a procedure as a structured argument while keeping study distinct from personal guidance.

sessions.title: Recall the Gemara’s question
sessions.translation: From where are these matters derived?
sessions.prompt: What does this question seek?
answers: The textual basis from which the matters are derived.
The person who first performed the procedure.
The final practical ruling for a modern case.
sessions.feedback: You can recognize when Gemara asks for the textual basis of an established procedure.

zevachim.kicker: KODASHIM SOURCE TRAIL · VALIDITY, INTENTION, OBLIGATION
zevachim.title: Read a case where “valid” does not yet mean “complete.”
zevachim.intro: Zevachim opens with offerings performed with the wrong intention. Follow the distinction between validity and fulfilling an obligation, then test why the Gemara needs both categories.

sessions.title: An offering with the wrong intention
sessions.translation: All offerings slaughtered not for their proper purpose.
sessions.prompt: What pressure does the Mishnah’s opening create?
answers: It asks what changes when a ritual act is done with a mismatched intention.
It describes a Temple act with no legal consequence.
It says intention never matters in any source.
sessions.feedback: Right. The case turns on the relationship between the act performed and the purpose named for it.

sessions.title: The act can remain valid
sessions.translation: Valid.
sessions.prompt: What does the Mishnah’s validity category ask the reader to keep distinct?
answers: Whether the act stands as valid apart from whether it achieves every intended result.
Whether every valid act has already fulfilled every obligation.
Whether the source is only discussing a person’s private feeling.
sessions.feedback: Good. Validity answers one legal question; it does not settle every other question in the case.

sessions.title: Valid, but not fulfilling
sessions.translation: They did not count for the owners toward their obligation.
sessions.prompt: What is the Mishnah adding after it calls the offerings valid?
answers: A separate question: whether the act fulfills the owner’s obligation.
A denial that the act has any legal status at all.
A claim that intention no longer needs examination.
sessions.feedback: Exactly. The source distinguishes a valid act from an act that discharges the obligation at issue.

sessions.title: Two outcomes, not one
sessions.translation: Valid · obligation.
sessions.prompt: Why is it a mistake to collapse these two outcomes into one?
answers: The source uses each category to answer a different question about the same act.
Two legal categories always mean the source is contradicting itself.
The second category is only decorative language.
sessions.feedback: Right. A careful map preserves distinctions before deciding how the categories relate.

sessions.title: The opening needs explanation
sessions.translation: What is the reason?
sessions.prompt: What does a Gemara reason-question invite after a Mishnaic distinction?
answers: Ask what principle explains why the two outcomes are separated.
Choose the outcome that feels more intuitive.
Ignore the Mishnah’s exact wording.
sessions.feedback: Good. The Gemara turns a stated distinction into a question about its underlying logic.

sessions.title: Intention matters in a defined way
sessions.translation: For its purpose · not for its purpose.
sessions.prompt: What should a reader test after identifying an intention distinction?
answers: Which result the intention changes and which result the source leaves intact.
Whether intention must change every possible legal result.
Whether the act can be understood without its source context.
sessions.feedback: Yes. Scope is the key: the source marks a consequence without claiming it changes everything.

sessions.title: A historical ritual system
sessions.translation: To learn · to understand · to ask.
sessions.prompt: What is the responsible use of this Temple-service source?
answers: Study its categories and reasoning as historical textual literacy.
Treat it as instructions for performing contemporary ritual.
Avoid its legal reasoning because the Temple setting is historical.
sessions.feedback: Serious study can learn from a historical system without confusing it with current practice.

sessions.title: Map a two-outcome case
sessions.translation: Act · result · obligation · limit.
sessions.prompt: What is the best first map for a source where an act may be valid yet fail to fulfill a further requirement?
answers: State the act, name each outcome, then test what fact changes one but not the other.
Choose the more favorable outcome before reading the categories.
Treat validity and fulfillment as interchangeable.
sessions.feedback: You can now read a legal distinction without flattening distinct results into a single verdict.
